Continued site use signifies consent . <h> Site studied for proof of mass extinction 66M years ago <p> STARKVILLE , Miss . -- In a trench behind an apartment complex off Highway 182 in west Starkville , a team of paleontologists were gathering handfuls of 66 million-year-old fossils . <p> From fossilized moulds of snail shells to evidence of ammonites -- prehistoric shelled mollusks that University of New Mexico post-doctoral researcher James Witts said " looked a little bit like a squid shoved into a shell " -- the group hoped the finds would help contribute to an ever-growing picture of what marine life looked like in the oceans covering what is now Northeast Mississippi millions of years ago . <p> More specifically , they @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a mass extinction event wiped out 70 per cent of life on earth 66 million years ago . <p> The site shows the Cretaceous-Paleogene ( K-Pg ) boundary , formerly called the Cretaceous-Tertiary ( K-T ) boundary , a geologic layer in the earth 's crust denoting the time of that mass extinction event . It occurs at the end of the Cretaceous Period and begins the Paleocene Period . Fossils found in layers of earth beneath the K-Pg boundary represent life before the extinction event , while fossils above are life after . <p> " It 's a pretty dramatic change ( from Cretaceous to Paleocene ) , " said Mississippi State graduate student Joshua Broussard , whose research project for MSU geosciences professor Renee Clary is on how life changed during and after the event . " Literally an apocalypse . " <p> Broussard discovered one of the sites the team is excavating -- a creek on private property off Highway 182 -- last fall with George Phillips , the paleontology curator with the Museum of Natural Science in Jackson . Phillips has been working with fellow scientists @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Brooklyn College and the University of New Mexico on projects about the K-Pg boundary for about 10 years . Though they 've studied sites around the South and in Mississippi before , this is the first time they 've studied the event in the Golden Triangle . <p> " There are multiple projects , but they all kind of converge on the K-Pg boundary , " Phillips said . <p> EXTINCTION EVENT <p> Though there are several theories about what may have caused the extinction at the K-Pg boundary 66 million years ago , the most well-known -- and the one Witts , Broussard , Phillips and the rest of the team believe is likely correct -- is that a 10-kilometre wide asteroid hit the Yucatan Peninsula . <p> " The idea is that this impact happened and it blasted a load of debris into the atmosphere and caused very rapid and sudden climate change , " Witts said . " There was maybe a period of global darkness , maybe global wildfires as all that debris rained out back onto the surface of the planet . And of course @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's the other side of the Gulf of Mexico , what would have been this shallow seaway here covering Mississippi today . So when that impact happened , you would have had some really catastrophic things happening right here in this sort of locality -- maybe giant tsunami waves , huge earthquakes undoubtedly and then all of this debris raining out of the sky . " <p> It 's the event most well-known for wiping out the dinosaurs , but the team said it also wiped out the ammonites and other lifeforms , from microorganisms to larger animals . <p> The extinction of microorganisms and plants who could n't photosynthesize with the debris blocking out the sun would have cut off the food supply of larger creatures -- " like kicking out the base of a tower of Jenga blocks , " Broussard said . <p> " Within five minutes the world is changed , " Witts said . " This impact event happened , and all these processes that are happening are maybe happening really really quickly . " <p> " Dinosaur plans are ruined , " Phillips agreed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ year ? " Witts agreed laughing . <p> The sites in Starkville , and particularly the creek site off Highway 182 , is exciting for the team because there is so much evidence of the impact . The team has discovered sediment containing impact spherules , small beads of earth originally from the Yucatan which were blasted into the sky at the time of the asteroid impact and then fell to the surface in other parts of the world . <p> Scientists can also glean information from what they do n't find . <p> " When you look at these rocks ( above the K-Pg boundary ) , you do n't find any of these guys . They 're all dead , " Witts said , holding up a small , fossilized shell of an ammonite found below the K-Pg boundary . " Just a few little species of oyster and a pretty dead sea floor compared to this diversity that you see in these rocks ( from ) before . That 's how life is after ... this extinction . <p> " You can start to see in higher @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> A basic premise of archaeology and paleontology is that the deeper in the earth something is found , the older it is . The scientists can tell where in the earth 's crust the K-Pg boundary is because beneath it , the rock is a different shade than above . Scientists hope the differences in the finds from the layers -- those before , during and after the extinction event -- will tell them more about the mass extinctions , but also how life bounces back after one . <p> RELEVANCE TODAY <p> That 's an interesting question for scientists , because it 's relevant to today , when deforestation , climate change and other factors are changing the earth and causing many species to go extinct , the team said . <p> Phillips said it would be easy to couch paleontology as an " intellectual science " without much bearing on what 's going on now . Projects like this prove that 's not the case , he said , since they can show how life was affected during times of geologic unrest and climate change . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and other facts of biology in general -- studying extinctions -- paleontology , the study of the paleontological world , the fossil world , is a good way to get a handle on the idea of what 's going on today and what might happen with certain changes in the composition of the atmosphere or how we 're interrupting the flow of resources in the environment , " Phillips said . " Humans are using a lot of resources . I do n't want to harp on humans , but we have changed the landscape of the earth a lot . " <p> For example , Witts said , one of the changes likely brought about by the asteroid impact was ocean acidification , which is happening again today , albeit at a slower process . <p> " There 's a lot of concern right now about environmental change and even whether we 're going into another mass extinction event and biodiversity crisis , caused maybe by human activities , " he said . " By studying these ancient extinctions , we can actually see what happens to life on @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ have a period of biodiversity crisis . " <p> The team , whose last day is today , will take some of the fossils and rock samples back to their respective museums and universities for display or to analyze for microscopic changes they ca n't see with the naked eye , Phillips said . <p> The finds will be just one part of the research scientists are doing all over the country to learn more about the event . <p> " ( The partnership ) with this group gives me a way to contribute to the big picture , " he said . <p> Notice : Your email may not yet have been verified . @@51906245 <h> Employers should help workers struggling with child care during COVID-19 <p> When daycares and schools closed during the pandemic , it caused burdens for working parents , particularly mothers . What is the responsibility of organizations to employees with children struggling with child care issues ? ( Christopher Ryan/Unsplash ) <p> The media abounds with stories of how working parents across Canada are struggling with caring for their young children during the COVID-19 pandemic while daycares and schools closed or operated part-time . <p> So what is the responsibility of employers towards employees who have children during the pandemic ? Are organizations responsible for their employees , and if so , what does this responsibility involve ? <p> I examine these questions using the social connection model that the late Iris Marion Young , an American political theorist , developed in her book Responsibility for Justice . <h> Child care difficulties <p> Child care can be difficult to access . It can represent a substantial financial expense for parents relative to their salary . It can also be challenging to reach from where they live and work , and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ care that is difficult to access has serious consequences . For example , when the financial cost of child care is overwhelming , one parent stops working , entirely or partially , to care for the children . That parent is often the mother . <p> The lion 's share of child care still falls to women , taking them out of the running for professional leadership roles . ( Kevin Liang/Unsplash ) <p> Women , in fact , are still stereotyped as caregivers ; according to Statistics Canada , they do more unpaid care work than men . At the same time , they are less likely to do full-time paid work , and those who do work full-time earn lower pay and are less likely to be in leadership positions . <p> For lone working parents , most of whom are women , alternative accommodations for child care can be more challenging to find , and can require working part-time or stopping work , or relying on family members . <p> The consequences from difficult-to-access child care are unjust : individuals , more often women than men , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ do not have to make . <p> These injustices are structural because they are n't specific to one individual . Instead , they are widespread , since many individuals , more often women than men , are limited in how they can act due also to conditions like cultural rules and norms regarding child care . <h> Women most affected during COVID-19 <p> As the COVID-19 pandemic started to spread across Canada in March 2020 and daycares closed , structural injustices related to access to child care were exposed . <p> Women across Canada who had not already lost their work took over care work and stopped their paid work . <p> The social connection model is concerned with the responsibility not of an organization , but individuals in the organization . Their responsibility arises not because they 're to blame for past actions towards employees , but because they can contribute to unjust structures , typically unknowingly , as they go about their professional lives , making decisions and taking actions . <p> For example , business leaders make decisions about hiring , performance evaluation and promotion , which @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ norms and cultures . <p> But those rules , norms and cultures are often unjust -- for example , parental leave rules that differ based on gender and unconscious gender bias during performance evaluation . <h> Shared responsibilities <p> In the social connection model , the responsibility of individuals to address structural injustice towards employees is shared . <p> Because all individuals at an organization contribute through their daily practices to this structural injustice , no one can , single-handedly , solve structural injustice . Instead , responsibility can only be discharged collectively when employers and employees join forces . <p> Some people have a more significant role to play : those with more considerable decision-making powers and those with more extensive means since they are better-equipped to address injustice ( organizational leaders , for example ) , as well as those who know the injustice well because they witness or experience it ( for example , employees who are parents or child care associations ) . <p> Employees with children who are trying to juggle work and child care responsibilities should have a voice in decisions . ( Charles @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ care associations and parents can act together to appeal to the government to make childcare more accessible , a challenge that is still very real in Canada and that 's resulted in recent calls for action . <p> Hopefully , organizational leaders will step in and rise to the occasion . They have been able to work together to address other societal challenges , including climate change -- so why not the challenges faced by their employees when it comes to childcare , particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic ?

Brasseur is being honoured for breaking a glass ceiling at Mach 1.5 and becoming not just among the country&amp;rsquo ; s first female military pilots , but its very first fighter pilot when , nearly 30 years ago , she took the controls of a CF-18 Hornet. &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; The Pioneer Award , she says , is dearer to her than the Order of Canada she received in 1998. &amp;ldquo ; This one is from my peers . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Brasseur joined the Canadian Forces in 1972 , when her family was stationed at CFB Penhold in Alberta . She applied to become a Physical Education and Recreation Officer , but learned that that , too , was a man&amp;rsquo ; s job . &amp;ldquo ; When I joined , there were 95,000 members of the Forces , and the number of women was capped at 1,500. &amp;rdquo ; She was asked if she wanted instead to work in nursing or a pharmacy , which she declined . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; But after a summer lifeguarding , she signed up , taking basic training at CFB Cornwallis in Nova Scotia , after which she was assigned the trade of administration clerk . &amp;ldquo ; I was a typist , &amp;rdquo ; she says . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; After two weeks in the dental office of the Winnipeg base , she decided enough was enough . Bruce Deachman/Postmedia &lt;/em&gt;&lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;&lt;br /&gt; Timing was on her side . In 1970 , the Royal Commission on the Status of Women in Canada recommended lifting the cap of 1,500 servicewomen and opening up more trades to women . Brasseur was accepted to the program and posted to North Bay as an Air Weapons Controller . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; In 1979 , as part of a program integrating women into traditionally men&amp;rsquo ; s roles , she was accepted into a pilot training course , and on Feb. 13 , 1981 , she , along with Captains Nora Bottomley and Leah Mosher , received her wings . Brasseur was granted her request to become a flight instructor in Moose Jaw . After Minister of Defence Perrin Beatty announced in 1987 that all military roles , including combat ones , should be open to women , Brasseur wrote a memo to her career officer indicating her interest in flying fighter jets , which she was granted in June 1988 , along with Captain Jane Foster . A year later , they became not just Canada&amp;rsquo ; s first female fighter pilots , but the first , anywhere , since the Second World War , when Russian women flew fighters in combat . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We didn&amp;rsquo ; t know that we were the first women fighter pilots . I wish it had been more fun . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Sometimes you got used to it , sometimes you got tired of it , sometimes you got frustrated and sometimes you just accepted it . And the cause ( or group of causes ) remains a mystery , though many suspect the modern spread of pesticides has a leading role . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; So who cares about bugs ? &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; When the flying insects disappear , so do the birds that eat them . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Insects pollinate the plants to produce much of your food , from apples to corn that livestock eat . Agriculture Canada estimates that while bees are the main pollinators , other insects such as hoverflies pollinate about 39 per cent of agricultural plants . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; And birders have watched in alarm as populations of many insect-eaters have crashed in recent decades : Swifts , swallows , nighthawks , martins and , of course , flycatchers are all a tiny fraction of their former populations . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Bird Studies Canada , a major conservation group , says annual bird counts have shown declines of 50 to 70 per cent in many of these species , and it says a loss of insects is one likely cause . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; The disappearance of insects could cause other problems that we haven&amp;rsquo ; t even thought of yet . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; The trouble lies in measuring the change , since it&amp;rsquo ; s hard to find a bug census from the mid-1900s to compare with numbers today . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s unfortunately a little bit informal in terms of measurements , &amp;rdquo ; said Jeremy Kerr , an ecologist and insect scientist at the University of Ottawa . &amp;ldquo ; Like , &amp;lsquo ; How pasted did your windshield get ? &amp;rsquo ; is not a normal scientific measurement . What if I had taken 10 more minutes ? &amp;rdquo ; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; She left the military on a medical release in 2014 after 16 years of service , since managing her mental health was a full-time job . Slowly , she reclaimed pieces of her life . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Two years ago , she returned to work as an administrative assistant in the federal government . Mark Hamill ( @HamillHimself ) &lt;a href= " https : **33;5332;TOOLONG ... 21 , **33;5367;TOOLONG Postmedia ( Archived Content ) Thu , 21 Sep 2017 18:16:24 **45;5402;TOOLONG ... &amp; RegionGoogle is linking secret , court-protected names - including victim IDs - to online coveragehttps : **31;5449;TOOLONG ... src= " http : **34;5482;TOOLONG ... title= " " alt= " " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;5518;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1297993150310 " /&gt; **25;5548;TOOLONG ; s powerful search engine is defeating some court-ordered publication bans in Canada and undermining efforts to protect young offenders and victims . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Computer experts believe it&amp;rsquo ; s an unintended , &amp;ldquo ; mind-boggling&amp;rdquo ; consequence of Google search algorithms . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; In six high-profile cases documented by the Citizen , searching the name of a young offender or victim online pointed to media coverage of their court cases , even though their names do not appear anywhere in the news articles themselves . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; It&amp;rsquo ; s a curious anomaly that appears to apply primarily to results produced by Google&amp;rsquo ; s search engine . Similar searches in Bing and Yahoo ! do not link the protected names to news coverage with the same consistency . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Informed of the findings , a Google spokesperson said the company would take action based on individual complaints . &amp;ldquo ; If search results that violate local laws are brought to our attention , we&amp;rsquo ; ll remove them , &amp;rdquo ; Google Canada&amp;rsquo ; s Aaron Brindle said in a written statement . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; The problem was discovered by Citizen court reporter Gary Dimmock , who found that a Google search of a young offender&amp;rsquo ; s name linked to news articles about the youth&amp;rsquo ; s case . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;&lt;br /&gt; In that case , a Barrhaven youth was found guilty of making a series of fake bomb threats and 911 calls that triggered police SWAT team responses to schools , shopping malls and personal residences across North America . He was 16 at the time and , as a result , his identity was barred from publication by provisions of the Youth Criminal Justice Act . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Dimmock asked editors to investigate the situation and ensure that the newspaper hadn&amp;rsquo ; t accidentally encoded the youth&amp;rsquo ; s name onto its website. &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; That subsequent investigation found the problem did not lie with the newspaper or its online source code . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; There was also meta data to consider . Meta data includes various information fields that reporters or editors fill out to describe an article , its photos or its videos , but which is not visible to the public . Again , nowhere in the metadata did the name appear . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Further inquiries revealed a similar issue existed in at least five other high-profile Ottawa cases in which publication bans had been in effect , as well as in court cases in Montreal and Windsor . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Media outlets are privy to the names of people whose identities are protected by publication bans by virtue of having a reporter in the courtroom . &amp;nbsp ; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; A Google search for the name of an Ottawa-based RCMP officer convicted of confining , starving and abusing his son links to coverage of that court case . The officer&amp;rsquo ; s identity is protected by a judge&amp;rsquo ; s order designed to shield his son from publicity . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; The officer&amp;rsquo ; s name had never been reported by the Citizen or any other media outlet . The abused boy , now 15 , was never identified in any article published online . Yet a search of the boy&amp;rsquo ; s name produces results that link to coverage of the case . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; In another high-profile case , a 17-year-old was charged in November 2016 with a series of offences after local mosques , synagogues and a church were spray-painted with hateful graffiti . The young offender has never been named in online news articles , but a search of his name connects to them . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; In yet another case , searching the name of a 1970s sex-assault victim revealed court coverage of the trial of a Kingston teacher and Ontario Hockey League billet found to have abused him . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; In Windsor , former OHL player Ben Johnson was convicted last year of sexually assaulting a &amp;ldquo ; near comatose&amp;rdquo ; 16-year-old girl at a nightclub . The victim&amp;rsquo ; s name , protected by a publication ban , is now tied to online court coverage of the case . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; The Google feedback loop means that in select cases , court-ordered publication bans are being undermined . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Most online news articles are archived on the web without an expiry date , which means the pieces will exist there for years to come . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Potential employers , co-workers , friends , partners &amp;mdash ; anyone searching an individual&amp;rsquo ; s name &amp;mdash ; can therefore be linked to online coverage that exposes the individual&amp;rsquo ; s past . The situation allows what the court-ordered bans were designed to protect against . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Ottawa lawyer Michael Crystal said he believes Google&amp;rsquo ; s search results may violate Canadian law and open the company to a class-action lawsuit from those whose privacy has been violated . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s very frightening that so many people could have access to this information and it&amp;rsquo ; s virtually unprotected , &amp;rdquo ; said Crystal , a privacy and data breach specialist . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;ldquo ; In the battlefield of privacy law , it seems like we&amp;rsquo ; re always fighting a rearguard action in terms of protecting privacy . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Google&amp;rsquo ; s Aaron Brindle declined to answer questions about how the search engine can link a given name to court coverage that doesn&amp;rsquo ; t contain it . &amp;ldquo ; Hundreds of factors contribute to what search results appear for a given query , &amp;rdquo ; he said , &amp;ldquo ; including things like PageRank , the specific words that appear on websites , the freshness of content and your region . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Google co-founder Larry Page once described the perfect search engine as &amp;ldquo ; understanding exactly what you mean and giving you back exactly what you want . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; To that end , Google uses programming algorithms to instantly sort through trillions of web pages to produce the most relevant results . It handles more than 3.5 billion searches a day , and dominates the search engine landscape . &lt;br /&gt; &amp;nbsp ; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Algorithms 101&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;br /&gt; &lt;strong&gt;What is an algorithm ? &lt;/strong&gt;&lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; In simple terms , an algorithm is a set of precise , step-by-step instructions to accomplish a task . By telling a friend how to reach your house from across town , you&amp;rsquo ; re creating an algorithm . A recipe is an algorithm , so is the list of instructions to set up your new TV. &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;strong&gt;What is a computer algorithm ? &lt;/strong&gt;&lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; A computer algorithm is a set of instructions that automate the task you want a computer to perform . This logical set of rules &amp;mdash ; rooted in mathematics &amp;mdash ; allows a computer to solve problems quickly , efficiently and consistently : It means , for instance , that every time you use an accounting spreadsheet to make financial calculations , the correct answers are produced . If you do the same thing twice , you get the same results . The best algorithms are the most efficient , and reach the correct answer with the fewest steps . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;strong&gt;&lt;br /&gt; How do algorithms work ? &lt;/strong&gt;&lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Programming languages , such as Python , JavaScript and Ruby , are used to express algorithms in a form that can be read and understood by a computer . These languages are used to write the computer code that unleashes the power of an algorithm , and allows it to solve massive problems &amp;mdash ; quickly . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;strong&gt;What kind of problems can they solve ? &lt;/strong&gt;&lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Algorithms are at the heart of almost everything your computer does . When Google Maps finds you the best way to a hockey rink &amp;mdash ; identifying the fastest route from dozens of possibilities &amp;mdash ; algorithms are at work . Playing chess against the computer is based on a program that uses algorithms to predict the best possible response to every one of your moves . Search engines , which comb through billions of web pages to find the most relevant results , are also based on a complex set of algorithmic instructions . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;strong&gt;&lt;br /&gt; How does Google use algorithms in its search engine ? &lt;/strong&gt;&lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Google&amp;rsquo ; s search engine uses algorithms both to analyze the words you use in a search and to produce the results that most accurately answer your query . The algorithms interpret spelling mistakes , and assess words that have more than one meaning . Google has organized the internet into a massive index . Its alogrithms comb that index to match keywords , while also ranking pages based on those with the most relevant and relied upon content . The algorithms instantly analyze hundreds of factors , including the &amp;ldquo ; freshness&amp;rdquo ; of the content , the number of other important websites that link to it , your location and your search history . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; The company is constantly refining its algorithms so that its searches do not simply return pages with the most matching &amp;ldquo ; keywords , &amp;rdquo ; but rather those with the most relevant information . Last year alone , Google made 1,600 tweaks to its search engine algorithm . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; A former company executive has revealed Google search results are sometimes informed by common search patterns . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; In May 2012 , Amit Singhal , then a Google senior vice-president , wrote a blog post to unveil major changes to the search engine that tapped into the &amp;ldquo ; collective intelligence of the web . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We can now sometimes help answer your next question before you&amp;rsquo ; ve asked it because the facts we show are informed by what other people have searched for , &amp;rdquo ; Singhal wrote . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; The inner workings of Google&amp;rsquo ; s search formula is a closely guarded secret . But based on publicly available information , it&amp;rsquo ; s possible to make educated guesses about how publication bans are being thwarted . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; In some cases &amp;mdash ; including the case of the young Ottawa swatter &amp;mdash ; a protected name was used in social media or in a blog by private individuals &amp;ndash ; not media outlets &amp;ndash ; that described the incident in question and linked to coverage . Evidence suggests Google&amp;rsquo ; s algorithm learns to associate web pages with search queries when a link to the page frequently appears alongside a particular phrase . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Some people have used the algorithm to make mischief . For example , in a co-ordinated effort launched by a political blogger in 2003 , the search terms &amp;ldquo ; miserable failure&amp;rdquo ; linked to pages about then-U.S. president George W. Bush . The results-altering practice became known as &amp;ldquo ; Google bombing . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Other publication ban cases are harder to explain , particularly those in which a protected name has never appeared anywhere on the web in connection to a crime . Such is the case for the unnamed RCMP officer found guilty of abusing his son . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Aristides Gionis , a computer science professor at Finland&amp;rsquo ; s Aalto University , suggested the search results may be influenced by common search patterns . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; For example , people who know or suspect they know the identity of someone whose name is covered by a publication ban might search for terms such as &amp;ldquo ; John Doe RCMP Ottawa child abuse&amp;rdquo ; and click on links to articles about the case . If enough people do that , the search engine might learn to associate those articles with searches for &amp;ldquo ; John Doe , &amp;rdquo ; even though the name does not appear in the article . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Search engines are smart enough to learn some hidden associations &amp;hellip ; but not smart enough to know that the associations should not be used in certain cases , &amp;rdquo ; explained Gionis , an expert in data mining and algorithmic data analysis . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; **25;5575;TOOLONG bans : A **31;5602;TOOLONG &lt;p&gt;&lt; ... /&gt; &lt;strong&gt;What is a publication ban ? &lt;/strong&gt;&lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; A publication ban is a court order that prohibits anyone from publishing , broadcasting or transmitting information that identifies an individual involved in the justice system . There are different kinds of bans . Some are meant to protect the integrity of a court case before trial , others the privacy of a victim or witness , and still others safeguard the identity of a young offender. &lt;br /&gt; &lt;strong&gt;&lt;br /&gt; What legislation is at work ? &lt;/strong&gt;&lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Canada has an open courts system , but both federal and provincial laws impose limits on what the media can publish . The Criminal Code , the Youth Criminal Justice Act , the Mental Health Act and the Child and Family Services Act all have provisions for publication bans that protect the names of individuals involved in the system . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;strong&gt;&lt;br /&gt; How are bans used in criminal proceedings ? &lt;/strong&gt;&lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Publication bans are often imposed early in court proceedings to ensure that potential jurors are not tainted by evidence heard during bail hearings , preliminary hearings and voir dires &amp;mdash ; hearings conducted during a trial to assess the admissibility of certain evidence . Judges can also impose publication bans to protect the names of witnesses or sexual assault victims . They also have the power to impose publication bans whenever required to ensure the &amp;ldquo ; proper administration of justice . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;strong&gt;How do publication bans apply to young offenders ? &lt;/strong&gt;&lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; The Youth Criminal Justice Act applies to anyone who was under 18 at the time of an alleged offence . One of the law&amp;rsquo ; s fundamental principles is that the identity of a young person should be protected in order make rehabilitation easier . The offender&amp;rsquo ; s identity can sometimes be published if the court imposes an adult sentence . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;strong&gt;&lt;br /&gt; How has the internet affected publication bans ? &lt;/strong&gt;&lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; The internet and social media have complicated publication bans , and made them difficult to police . In 2012 , for instance , the federal government conceded its longstanding publication ban on early election results could not survive the internet age : It lifted an election night blackout on Atlantic Canada returns that had stood since 1938. &amp;ldquo ; The ban &amp;hellip ; does not make sense with widespread use of social media and modern communications technology , &amp;rdquo ; said Tim Uppal , then minister of state for democratic reform . The ban was in place to ensure that all Canadians cast their ballots without being influenced by early results . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; University of Toronto computer science professor Periklis Andritsos , a data-mining expert , said he could not isolate a technical explanation for the phenomenon . &amp;ldquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s mind boggling , &amp;rdquo ; he said . &amp;ldquo ; I would like to be able to say 100 per cent this is it , but I can&amp;rsquo ; t. &amp;rdquo ; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; The best theory Andritsos could offer is that a critical number of people have used the protected name alongside similar search terms , thereby establishing a pattern of links to news coverage . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;ldquo ; If there are a lot of links pointing to these sites , it could be the case , &amp;rdquo ; he said . &amp;ldquo ; It must be accidental , but I can&amp;rsquo ; t find explanations for it . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Montreal lawyer Allen Mendelsohn said the case involves an untested area of the law since no one employed by Google would know the protected names . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It must be Google&amp;rsquo ; s technology figuring things out on its own , scraping information in an artificially intelligent way , &amp;rdquo ; said Mendelsohn , an internet law specialist who teaches privacy law at McGill University . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;ldquo ; This could be a violation of a publication ban , but whether it is or not is a bit more complicated because Google is not seen as a publisher , per se , and that adds complexity to the situation . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;p&gt;Most guys are trying to get out of the notorious Ottawa jail , but not young Damian O'Reilly. &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; He was actually pretty desperate to get inside the Ottawa-Carleton Detention Centre after hatching a drug-smuggling plot that would see marijuana sold to inmates for 10 times its street value . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; All he had to do was find a crack in the system , some sure-fire way of getting arrested and jailed . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; And it had to be quick , for O'Reilly , 20 , had &amp;quot ; hooped&amp;quot ; not one , not two , but eight Kinder Surprise eggs filled with marijuana , tobacco , matches and rolling papers before setting out to get arrested on June 19 , 2016. &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; The Italian chocolate egg treat that comes with a toy inside ( assembly required ) is one of the most popular ways of smuggling contraband into Canadian jails . The yolk-coloured plastic capsule that holds the surprise toy is thin and flexible , making it easier to ' hoop ' &amp;mdash ; a jail term for inserting contraband into your rectum. &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; O'Reilly figured the quickest way to get arrested would be to throw a rock at a police cruiser in front of the courthouse and , sure enough , he got the job done in minutes flat . It helped that he was already on probation , so when he was arrested , he was held for bail and shipped off to the old Innes Road jail . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; And that 's where his plot unravelled . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; It 's not known if the guard noticed O'Reilly was in some discomfort but whatever the reason , the guard had suspicions that O'Reilly might be smuggling drugs . The young inmate was escorted to dry cell No. 9 . A dry cell has no plumbing and guards will either attempt to seize the contraband or wait for it to be expelled . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; In this case , it was O'Reilly himself who , once alone in the dry cell , removed eight Kinder Surprise eggs from his rectum . A guard had to then collect the eggs and photograph them before securing them inside the Ottawa police drug safe at the jail . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; In all , the eight eggs contained 59 grams of marijuana , a gram of MDMA , tobacco , rolling papers and matches . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; O'Reilly pleaded guilty to drug trafficking and was sentenced Monday to two years , less 250 days credited for pre-trial custody . His failed smuggling attempt is documented in an agreed statement of facts filed in court . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Defence lawyer Paolo Giancaterino praised his young client 's efforts to improve himself since his arrest . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;quot ; Damian has been working hard to turn his life around . He is a young man who is aiming to be a productive member of our community when he is released , &amp;quot ; Giancaterino said . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; O'Reilly 's hooping of eight Kinder Surprise eggs is believed to be a record in criminal defence and jailhouse circles , with the closest recorded feat coming in at just four eggs back in 2010. &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; A year earlier , in 2009 , and also at the Ottawa jail , inmate Gregory Ingram , 33 , choked on a Kinder Surprise egg filled with drugs and later died at hospital . It was a strip search at the Innes Road jail that led to his death in the early morning hours of June 21 , 2009 . The guards noticed that he reached into his underwear and then brought a closed fist to his mouth , according to an inquest . It was obvious that he was trying to hide the drugs in his mouth . Paramedics later discovered the yellow plastic egg lodged in his throat . They were able to remove it , but not before Ingram&amp;rsquo ; s brain was deprived of oxygen long enough to be left in a&amp;nbsp ; permanent vegetative state . He died three days later after his family removed him from life support . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; In that case , the drugs were smuggled for personal use . But in O'Reilly 's case , the drugs were bound for the lucrative jailhouse market , where drug debts are usually paid in e-transfers to third parties . Each customer is given a numerical identifier and when their third-party representative makes the transfer , the number associated with the customer is included in the cents column of the transfer amount , making it easy to track payments . It is not known if O'Reilly was forced to smuggle in the drugs at someone 's behest or if he was acting alone . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Shutting down smuggling into Ontario jails is something the province has spent money on recently . A body scanner machine &amp;mdash ; a 918-kilogram device that takes a high-definition picture of an inmate standing on a moving platform that passes through a narrow X-ray beam &amp;mdash ; was installed in the Ottawa jail on Aug. 29 , 2016 . She was also the granddaughter of a Polish-born Holocaust survivor , and as part of her attempt to understand that past , she enrolled in a Canadian Jewish Studies class taught by Prof. Rebecca Margolis. &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; During a project that examined international reaction to the wartime genocide that killed almost two out of every three European Jews , Grosman discovered that Canada was the only Allied power not to have a Holocaust memorial in its capital . She was outraged , especially considering that only Israel and the United States were home to more Holocaust survivors . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;quot ; This is absurd . How is that even possible ? &amp;quot ; Grosman asked her professor . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;quot ; I do n't have an answer for you , &amp;quot ; Margolis said . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Grosman pursued answers . The second-year university student met with members of the Jewish community and reached out to federal politicians . She learned that previous attempts had been made to establish a monument without success . &amp;quot ; All of the answers about why we did n't have a monument , none of them were good enough , &amp;quot ; she said . &amp;quot ; So I said , ' Alright , I 've got to get to work . I felt very strongly that this needed to happen . ' &amp;quot ; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Grosman had studied government . She decided that her best chance rested with a private member 's bill &amp;mdash ; legislation introduced by an individual member of Parliament . Only a small fraction of such bills ever get passed into law . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Grosman approached her local MP , Liberal Susan Kadis . The then Thornhill MP agreed to draft the bill , but told Grosman she would have to &amp;quot ; do all the work&amp;quot ; to get it passed . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Still a teenager , Grosman lobbied political staffers and MPs to build support . &amp;nbsp ; &amp;quot ; I had a lot of people telling me , ' No , ' saying there were more important things or other things on their agendas . But I did n't stop . &amp;quot ; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; The first bill died on the order paper when Parliament was dissolved in September 2008 for a federal election that returned Prime Minister Stephen Harper to power . In Thornhill , Kadis lost her seat to Conservative Peter Kent . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Grosman met Kent , and the former journalist and news anchor agreed to champion the project . But Kent was immediately appointed to cabinet , which precluded him from introducing a private member 's bill , so he approached newly elected Tory MP Tim Uppal , who held a favourable number on the order paper . ( It meant that his proposed legislation would be among the first to be considered by the House of Commons. ) &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Uppal , a Sikh from Edmonton , agreed to sponsor what would become known as Bill-442. &amp;quot ; I look on it as something I did as a Canadian : Canada needed this , &amp;quot ; said Uppal , who worked with Grosman to build all-party support . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;quot ; I found her to be so determined , &amp;quot ; Uppal said . &amp;nbsp ; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; They met with Liberal , NDP and Bloc Quebecois MPs. &amp;nbsp ; &amp;quot ; I did n't want this to be a political issue , &amp;quot ; said Grosman. &amp;quot ; I wanted everyone to stand up and support it . It was very important to me that that happened . &amp;quot ; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; The bill went through the transport committee because then transport minister John Baird was responsible for the National Capital Commission , which was donating land for the project . The bill was delayed as MPs debated who should pay for it . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Opposition MPs felt the government should finance all of the monument , but Canadian Jewish groups wanted to pay half . Ultimately , that 's the plan that was accepted . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Peter Kent also enlisted Harper 's support for the project , and in March 2010 , the Speech from the Throne included a government commitment to establish a national Holocaust memorial . The bill passed the Commons with all-party support , but still needed to clear the Senate at a time when Harper 's government was in crisis . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; It raced through two final readings in a week , and was given Royal Assent hours before the government fell in a non-confidence vote on March 25 , 2011. &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;quot ; I was a wreck , &amp;quot ; Grosman remembered . &amp;quot ; I was terrified that after all of the work , and all of the hours and hours that went into it , that it was just going to die again . According to Ontario figures , since the federal law came into effect in June 2016 , 55 per cent of assisted deaths were in hospitals . Only six per cent were residents in long-term care , such as Extendicare Starwood , where Hopkins was the first resident to die with medical assistance . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; In greater Ottawa ( the Champlain Local Health Integration Network ) , there were between 61 and 78 cases to the end of June , with 46 of those in The Ottawa Hospital . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Hopkins , who died on Aug. 7 at the age of 85 , did not have a significant problem finding a physician to perform the service , though there are only four medical providers registered with the Champlain LHIN. &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Nor was there an issue with her eligibility , though this can be a sticking point . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; According to the law , a person must have a &amp;ldquo ; grievous and irremediable medical condition , &amp;rdquo ; which it proceeds to define in four bullet points , the most contentious being : &amp;ldquo ; Be at a point where your natural death has become reasonably foreseeable . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; A person need not have a terminal condition but must &amp;ldquo ; experience unbearable physical or mental suffering from your illness &amp;hellip ; that can not be relieved under conditions that you consider acceptable . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Hopkins ended up being referred to Dr. Paul Irwin , who assessed her independently in the fall of 2016 , saw her again in the spring and agreed to perform the procedure on her chosen day . ( The law requires two written opinions of eligibility and the physician or nurse practitioners must be &amp;ldquo ; independent&amp;rdquo ; of each other. ) &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;ldquo ; There&amp;rsquo ; s no question , &amp;rdquo ; the condition of cerebellar ataxia would have eventually killed her , he said , adding he was struck at how much she declined in the months he knew her . Jo Hopkins was made of braver **30;9360;TOOLONG &lt;p&gt;It was an honour to be asked to tell the life story of Josephine &amp;ldquo ; Jo&amp;rdquo ; Hopkins , who , with eyes wide open , bravely wrote her own ending . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; What I didn&amp;rsquo ; t anticipate , was its power to invade . David Vivian Currie , a hero of Normandy . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;quot ; The medal did n't define who my grandfather was , &amp;quot ; he said . &amp;quot ; People read the history about what happened in the action . I remember him as the man who put my chain back on my bike when it fell off ... or doing his painting or sitting in the car waiting for my grandmother and doing his crossword puzzles . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;quot ; I knew what he did and obviously he was an important person , but in my life he was my grandfather &amp;mdash ; and a hero &amp;mdash ; grandfather first though . &amp;quot ; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Currie 's VC , Canada 's highest honour for bravery in battle , is going on auction next month in London , England , along with his&amp;nbsp ; campaign stars and other service medals . Currie 's widow , Isabel , sold them to a private collector after his death in 1986 at the age of 74 . The opening bid for the VC is $500,000. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;Currie was awarded the VC for leading a small battle group of Canadian tanks and infantry that blocked an encircled German army from escaping the Falaise Pocket in August 1944 . His is one of only 12 VCs awarded to Canadians in Canadian units during the Second World War . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Currie was later named Sergeant of Arms of the House of Commons . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; News that the medal will be sold at auction has led to calls for the sale of military medals to be banned . That would be a mistake , says Tanya Ursual , whose company , Medals of War , is the Canadian agent for London auction house Dix Noonan Webb . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;quot ; I understand that people are emotional when it comes to military medals . They are significant artifacts that connect to a different time in a different way . But the reality is they are a good that are a part of our economic system , &amp;quot ; says Ursual , who arranged for David Currie to have a private viewing of his grandfather 's medals at the bank where they are stored . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;quot ; In Canada , military medals remain private property and as such as part of our rights we should be able to sell our property when we choose . &amp;quot ; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; The Victoria Cross is one of the rarest medals in the world . Just 1,358 have been awarded to British and Commonwealth armed forces members since it was established by Queen Victoria in 1856 . Ninety-four Canadians have been awarded the VC , although not all were serving in Canadian units . In contrast , there have been 3,499 recipients of the U.S. Medal of Honor , that nation 's highest award for bravery . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; The U.S. outlawed the sale and trade of the Medal of Honor in 1923 . Anyone convicted faces a fine of up to $100,000 and/or up to a year in jail . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; The Federal Bureau of Investigation even has a special agent who investigates illegal sales or individuals who pose as Medal of Honor recipients . The law has n't stopped sales , however , with many being smuggled out of the country and offered for sale on foreign websites . It does n't help that the market is awash with counterfeits , some even made and sold by the company that was the official supplier to the U.S. government . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; The U.S. law even prevents the Congressional Medal of Honor Society , which runs a museum in Charleston , S.C. , from buying up legitimate medals that are on the open market . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;quot ; The risk is when you prohibit or prevent the sale of an item , you often make it more seductive , &amp;quot ; Ursual said . &amp;quot ; You drive it into an underground market and an underground economy . The items disappear , then they appear somewhere else in the world at a greatly inflated price . It moves medals out of our safe market and into an international market where they become even more elusive , more valuable which makes it even more difficult to buy them back . &amp;quot ; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; The Currie family hopes the medals are bought by a public institution , such as the Canadian War Museum , or by a private collector who might donate them to the public . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;The current owner bought them from Isabel Currie in 1989 and has cherished them , even travelling three times to Owen Sound to visit Lt.-Col. Currie 's grave , Ursual said . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;quot ; He loved those medals almost as much as he loved your grandfather , &amp;quot ; she told David Currie. &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; If sold to a foreign buyer , the medals would not be allowed to leave Canada without an export permit and that could n't happen until a Canadian buyer or institution has been given a chance to purchase them from the new owner at an acceptable price . &lt;br /&gt; But an agency within his own ministry known as the Government Operation Centre ( GOC ) is tasked with coordinating the efforts of all the different agencies . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;When asked why information about the operation was so unreliable if GOC was supposed to be coordinating everything , Goodale blamed it on the initial chaos of setting up such a large housing operation in a very short amount of time . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;&amp;ldquo ; I think it was because the situation developed so rapidly and I think everyone recognized that in the discussion today , &amp;rdquo ; said Goodale. &amp;ldquo ; What&amp;rsquo ; s required here is not the pre-emption of responsibilities by one agency over another ; it&amp;rsquo ; s the seamless coordination of all of them together , and a single point of contact . And we have provided that . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;For all of the efforts to provide accurate information to the public on the situation in the past few days , one question that has still not been completely answered is how long the asylum seekers will continue to be sent to Cornwall . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;According to Goodale , the asylum seekers will continue to come to Cornwall for as long as there is a need for extra housing facilities . Once they have been given a date to appear before the quasi-judicial refugee committee , they will be moved out of the Nav Centre and into more normal housing arrangements to wait for their hearing . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;When asked where this housing will be located , Goodale said the Quebec and Ontario governments were handling that issue . &lt;/p&gt; Alan S. Historic Canadian Victoria Cross up for auctionhttps : **32;11248;TOOLONG ... src= " http : **34;11282;TOOLONG ... title= " " alt= " " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;11318;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1297984866450 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt;In the famous photograph , Maj. David Currie holds a pistol in his right hand as several vanquished Germans soldiers march past , their arms raised in surrender . It is Aug. 19 , 1944 and Currie and his small battle group of Sherman tanks and infantrymen have held fast under 36 hours of constant attacks from a trapped and desperate German army . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;The image is , in the words of the army 's official historian C.P. Stacey , &amp;quot ; as close as we are ever likely to come to a photograph of a man winning the Victoria Cross . &amp;quot ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;Now that Victoria Cross is for sale . Starting bid ? $500,000 . The sale takes place Sept. 27 in London through the auctioneer , Dix Noonan Webb&lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;&amp;quot ; It 's a very rare occurrence , &amp;quot ; says&amp;nbsp ; Tanya Ursual , a military antiquarian in Kemptville who is acting as the auction house 's Canadian agent . In 27 years in the business , Ursual says , she 's handled about 10 Victoria Crosses through her company , Medals of War . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;Currie 's story is special , she says . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;&amp;quot ; It 's the kind of things movies are made of , except it 's a real story . In spite of all odds , in the face of enormous danger , you make a choice that you will not be defeated . &amp;nbsp ; He 's a Canadian hero who , arguably , changed the course of the war . &amp;quot ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;Currie 's VC was one of only 12 awarded to Canadians fighting in a Canadian units in the Second World War and the only Canadian VC from the bitter fighting of D-Day and Normandy . The simple bronze cross , embossed with ' For Valour ' and hung from a plain purple ribbon , is the&amp;nbsp ; British Commonwealth 's highest award for gallantry in the face of the enemy . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;A native of Sutherland , Sask. , Currie worked as a mechanic and welder before the war and had only had 10 days of combat experience before being ordered to hold a key road leading out of the Falaise Pocket where a German army lay trapped . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;&amp;quot ; During the next 36 hours the Germans hurled one counter-attack after another against the Canadian force but so skilfully had Major Currie organised his defensive position that these attacks were repulsed with severe casualties to the enemy after heavy fighting , &amp;quot ; his official citation reads . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;&amp;quot ; Throughou ... three days and nights of fierce fighting , Major Currie&amp;rsquo ; s gallant conduct and contempt for danger set a magnificent example to all ranks of the force under his command . &amp;quot ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;&amp;qu ... blocking action there is unbelievable , &amp;quot ; said Tim Cook , a historian at the Canadian War Museum and author of a two-volume history of Canadians in the Second World War . &amp;quot ; This is closing the Falaise Gap . You 've got hundreds of thousands of soldiers fighting away and it all comes to Currie and this small battle groups of the South Alberta Regiment and the Argyll and Sutherland Highlanders holding this small town . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;&amp;quot ; The Germans are fighting for their lives . They 're in this collapsing pocket and they 're being torn apart by artillery and Typhoons ( fighter bombers ) . There 's this tremendous sense of desperation on the part of the Germans . &amp;quot ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;Over the course of the battle , Currie 's force inflicted 800 casualties , destroyed seven tanks and took 2,100 prisoners . Currie 's force took heavy casualties too . Every other officer in his command was killed or wounded . Currie himself slept for only one hour during the entire battle . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;After the war , Currie went to work with a pulp and paper company but in 1959 was appointed Sergeant at Arms by prime minister John Diefenbaker . He and his wife , Isabel , lived quietly in Riverview Park until his death on June 24 , 1986. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;Isabel sold his medals after his death , said grandson David Currie . Isabel Currie is 105 and now lives in an Ottawa nursing home . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;&amp;quot ; It was always a bit of a family secret , but the money she got is what is supporting her now and the good care she is getting , &amp;quot ; the younger David Currie said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;The family only learned of the auction a few days ago . Isabel is the only person who knows who the buyer was , he says . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;Ursual would not identify the medal 's current owner . &amp;nbsp ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;&amp;quot ... client would appreciate my respecting his privacy as much as possible , &amp;quot ; she said . &amp;quot ; He has n't given me a reason for his decision to sell . Certainly he was in contact with the family when he purchased the medals from them and he has been a great steward of those medals and loved them and cared for them . &amp;quot ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;The sale is taking place in England , but the medals ca n't be taken out of the country without an export permit because they are considered cultural property . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;The export rule does n't stop a foreign buyer from purchasing the medals , so long as they stay in Canada . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p class= " p1 " &gt;&amp;quot ; A wealthy benefactor could potentially purchase them and donate them to a Canadian organization , &amp;quot ; she said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p class= " p1 " &gt;&amp;quot ; In my 27 years in the business , I have seen all types of clients . @@51907114 <h> DEEP DIVE : Building back better with Canadian biosphere reserves <p> This brief is one of a series produced by the Building Back Better Post-COVID-19 Task Force , a group of experts and partners affiliated with the Canadian Commission for UNESCO and its UNESCO Chairs Network . Their goal is to bring together sustainable economic recovery ideas to make our communities stronger in a post-COVID-19 world . <p> The series highlights how responding to the COVID-19 crisis through adaptive and strategic infrastructure investments can preserve critical ecosystems , increase the use of green infrastructure , and protect regional resources and distribution systems . These infrastructures can meet basic human needs and improve human health , while fostering long-term community resilience , well-being and sustainable employment . <p> The suggestions offered in this series support Canada 's commitments to the UN Agenda 2030 Sustainable Development Goals and position the country as a world leader in developing new economies based on environmental sustainability . <p> Building back better with Canadian biosphere reserves <p> The COVID-19 crisis has changed the day-to-day lives of people all around the globe . While the pandemic @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ these changes have benefited the environment , and the planet as a whole . As many stay home , work remotely , and commute less , the resulting decreases in air and noise pollution have already positively affected our surroundings . It is crucial that the resulting impacts are not quickly turned aside , and that we seize the opportunity to promote a greener , more resilient , and more sustainable society . The 18 biosphere reserves in Canada that have been designated by UNESCO help to preserve the unique ecosystems and biodiversity of our country for present and future generations . These biosphere reserves are ideally positioned to build more resilient and sustainable communities in the post-COVID-19 era . Because they play a key role in mobilizing local partners , biosphere reserves can be used to initiate and pilot sustainable solutions and support a wide range of activities through engagement , collaboration and project development . The mobilization of partnerships and their sustainable activities can be leveraged in future . <p> Context <p> Nearly 2.5 million people live in Canada 's 18 biosphere reserves . They work to promote the conservation of biological and cultural diversity while promoting economic and social development . In each biosphere reserve , community partners work together to find innovative ways to achieve a balance between the needs of humans and nature . This is accomplished by working together to develop and implement new projects , create new resources , and facilitate positive change in conserving biodiversity , sustainable development , sustainable tourism , research and education , adaptation to climate change , and reconciliation . The relationships and partnerships they form within their regions builds a sense of place and community . <p> Through engagement with key local and regional stakeholders , biosphere reserves play an essential role in accelerating sustainable , community-led transformations . Contributed photo <p> NEWS RELEASE LAKEHEAD UNIVERSITY **25;2528;TOOLONG Jacob Kearey-Moreland was contributing to campus life long before he was a Lakehead University student . <p> This year 's recipient of the Lloyd Dennis Award for outstanding citizenship , Kearey-Moreland has been a driving force behind local community gardening initiatives for over a decade -- from Toronto during his undergraduate degree , through community advocacy in Orillia , and now as a graduate student at Lakehead . <p> A grassroots champion for social and ecological justice , he 's helping secure people 's right to collectively produce and access food , while also preserving public , multi-generational spaces to gather , learn , exercise , and interact . <p> " Community gardening is as much about growing a community as it is producing food , " says Kearey-Moreland , who grew up on a farm in Simcoe County and now co-owns Bass Lake Farms in Oro-Medonte . " It 's like a communal outlet people can @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ together . " <p> On the Orillia campus , a number of community efforts Kearey-Moreland has helped bring to life are easily spotted : the butterfly garden , the traditional Three Sisters garden , the Four Directions teaching garden , and the community and allotment vegetable gardens are all in view from the large windows of the central Learning Commons . <p> In the background , he also dedicates countless hours to fundraising , event planning , public speaking , advocacy , and outreach . Making good use of social media , strategic networking , and farming-based puns , he 's adept at rallying volunteers with enthusiasm , humour , and information . <p> And the benefit to students , faculty , staff , and the wider community is clear : university classes , Indigenous ceremonies , and community tours all regularly take place in the gardens , food is produced all summer , and the seeds generated are made freely available in the library . The Lakehead Farm Club Kearey-Moreland founded is now one of the largest student clubs on campus , which he says speaks to gardening 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ food insecurity , isolation and poverty , and they want a more sustainable campus with more recreation opportunities -- gathering outside to socialize and produce your own food solves all those problems . " <p> Kearey-Moreland 's current focus is his Master of Education -- a program with online , flexible formats that allow him to continue farming . His thesis on garden-based learning complements the ideas he pilots on his farm , including hosting school groups and creating youth employment opportunities . <p> " I want to be part of the societal shift where we teach kids about climate change and food insecurity but also give them the tools to feed their families and communities and work together to sustain life and ecosystems . " <p> Looking ahead , Kearey-Moreland hopes to translate his degree and community service into making the Lakehead Orillia campus an influential hub for garden-based learning . In the meantime , his initiatives are in even higher demand in the new reality created by COVID-19 . <p> " Community gardening certainly is n't new -- it 's something humans have been doing for 10,000 years @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for many of us to reflect on what is important to healthy societies , ecosystems and economies , and ultimately how we want to be able to grow and access our food , " he said . <p> Lakehead University 's Lloyd Dennis Award for outstanding citizenship is presented annually to a full-time student at the Orillia campus in recognition of their contributions to the welfare of the university through their student activities . <p> The award is named in honour of the late Lloyd Dennis , an Officer of the Order of Canada and Order of Ontario . He was a highly respected educator and author , best remembered for the 1968 landmark report that shaped the future of education in Ontario -- Living and Learning : The Report of the Provincial Committee on Aims and Objectives of Education in the Schools of Ontario , known as the Hall-Dennis Report . An enthusiastic proponent of the Lakehead Orillia campus , in 2009 Dennis was honoured with Lakehead 's Civitas Award and then in 2012 with a Doctor of Laws ( posthumously ) . <p> We welcome your feedback and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ you be respectful of others and their points of view , refrain from personal attacks and stay on topic . Ottawa&lt;p&gt;New and startling evidence of Google 's ability to possibly defeat court-ordered publication bans has emerged as an Ottawa law firm prepares a class-action lawsuit against the search engine giant . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; The Sun has found that , in two high-profile Ontario cases , Google searches aimed at finding online news coverage of the trials will return &amp;quot ; related searches&amp;quot ; that include the names of individuals shielded by the courts . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; These inadvertent disclosures provide fresh examples of how Google could be undermining court-ordered publication bans put in place to protect crime victims and young offenders . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Meanwhile , Ottawa lawyer Michael Crystal said he intends to launch a class-action lawsuit on behalf of those whose right to remain anonymous may have been breached by&amp;nbsp ; Google search algorithms . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;quot ; I am quite concerned this violation may create a chill in the court process if not confronted , &amp;quot ; Crystal said . &amp;quot ; Complainants in sexual assault matters often come forward on the basis that their identities will be protected . &amp;quot ; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; In recent weeks , the Sun has discovered that Google 's powerful search engine can link a protected name to court coverage , and court coverage to a protected name . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; In one high-profile Ontario case , anyone using common search terms to retrieve news stories about the trial produces a list of &amp;quot ; related searches&amp;quot ; that includes the name of a protected sexual assault victim . In another much-publicized case , the &amp;quot ; related searches&amp;quot ; list includes the court-protected name of a child abuser. &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; It means that someone who does n't know the protected name of a victim or offender can , in certain cases , be linked to them through the &amp;quot ; related searches&amp;quot ; function . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Google 's list of related searches often appear at the bottom of a search page in dark blue hyperlinks. &amp;nbsp ; ( Related search links do not always appear : The search engine requires a&amp;nbsp ; certain volume of associated searches for it to trigger related search results. ) &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; The tool was first unveiled by Google in 2008 . In an official blog from the company 's Google News team , it was promoted as a way for web surfers to browse the news , &amp;quot ; perhaps finding connections between stories that you had n't seen . &amp;quot ; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;quot ; As is normal for Google News , &amp;quot ; the blog noted , &amp;quot ; there are no human editors involved in selecting related searches : These suggestions are automatically generated based on an algorithm to determine terms related to your search . &amp;quot ; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Google Canada officials reiterated Friday that they will act on individual complaints and remove search results that violate local laws . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; The latest developments follow a Sun story that revealed Google 's search engine can link the protected names of young offenders and victims to online media coverage . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Computer experts believe such links are an unintended consequence of math-based algorithms that can produce results informed by what other people have searched for online . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; In six high profile cases documented by the Sun , searching the name of a young offender or victim &amp;mdash ; shielded by court order &amp;mdash ; will return results with online media coverage of their court cases , even though their names do not appear anywhere in the news stories . The same held true for high profile cases in Montreal and Windsor . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; The problem was first discovered by Sun court reporter Gary Dimmock , who was troubled when he found that a Google search of a young offender&amp;rsquo ; s name linked to his stories . Dimmock asked editors to investigate the situation and ensure that the Sun hadn&amp;rsquo ; t accidentally encoded the youth&amp;rsquo ; s name onto the paper&amp;rsquo ; s website. &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; A subsequent investigation found the problem did not lie with the newspaper 's online source code or with the digital forms that reporters and editors use to describe stories and photos . Really ? &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;&amp;ldquo ; The Landmark Forum is a rollercoaster ride that provides an unprecedented and unpredictable adventure , &amp;rdquo ; Top 100 Expo describes . &amp;ldquo ; The &lt;a href= " http : **34;16859;TOOLONG ... target= " blank " &gt;Landmark Forum&lt;/a&gt; is about creating new possibilities for your life . It&amp;rsquo ; s totally transformational , not just exciting . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;The ranking sparked numerous responses from Landmark participants , who noted positive changes in their lives after the Landmark Forum courses . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;&amp;ldquo ; I went into Landmark thinking I will get some answers on how to manage my business in a more effective manner . Loved the rollercoaster ride of my life . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;So , what exactly is The Landmark Forum ? &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;The &lt;a href= " http : **34;16895;TOOLONG ... target= " blank " &gt;Landmark Forum&lt;/a&gt; is an intensive three-day course designed to guide participants to a personal breakthrough , while giving them new ways of looking at themselves and the world . Forum students learn to identify thought patterns that are holding them back and move beyond self-imposed limits created by fears and old habits . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;Forum participants claim the courses help them gain new insights into themselves , build better relationships with their families and improve their performance , effectiveness and creativity on a professional level . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;The Landmark Forum is one of a series of educational seminars presented by San Francisco-based Landmark , an organization founded in 1991 . Landmark&amp;rsquo ; s courses are based on theories about personal development and transformation , with more than 2.8 million people in 22 countries having taken part in the organization&amp;rsquo ; s various educational programs . High profile Landmark graduates include Chip Wilson , founder of Lululemon Athletica Inc. , radio personality Robin Quivers of &amp;ldquo ; The Howard Stern Show&amp;rdquo ; and composer Alan Menken. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;Over the years , journalists and freelance writers have attended Landmark Forum classes and have written detailed accounts about their experiences . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;In 2011 , &lt;a href= " http : **34;16931;TOOLONG ... target= " blank " &gt;Time magazine contributor Nathan Thornburgh&lt;/a&gt; signed up for the Landmark Forum . ' and started asking , ' Can they help what 's wrong with me ? ' I benefitted tremendously from the uncomfortable mirror that the course had put in front of me. &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;Some critics think the instructors are too tough or insensitive to participants ' unique circumstances . They are all extinct today . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; But these hyoliths didn&amp;rsquo ; t appear to fit the pattern of evolution of animals that came before them , or those that came after . Paleontology had a problem to solve . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; On Wednesday , a Canadian-British group provided a new look at the &amp;ldquo ; oddball&amp;rdquo ; hyolith , indicating that it does indeed fit the bigger jigsaw puzzle of life . Their work is published in the journal Nature . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; The fossils come largely from British Columbia&amp;rsquo ; s Burgess Shale , a former ocean bed where ancient life was covered and fossilized during frequent mudslides. &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Even though they are so widespread , we had absolutely no idea what they were , &amp;rdquo ; said paleontologist Martin Smith of Durham University . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;ldquo ; People talked about them as though they were a completely separate branch from the tree of life , &amp;rdquo ; he said . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Some scientists even thought they were their own phylum , meaning a major separate category of life . All mammals , birds , fish and reptiles are in a single phylum . Was a separate one needed just for these cone-shaped sea creatures ? &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; It isn&amp;rsquo ; t , Smith says now . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It turned out that sure , they have a pretty unusual morphology ( physical form ) , &amp;rdquo ; he said . &amp;ldquo ; But they are possible to relate to a modern group . They&amp;rsquo ; re not quite as weird as we might have thought . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; The key lay in finding fossils that preserved the softer parts of the hyolith . But unlike the territorial and aggressive chimps , bonobos are known as the &amp;lsquo ; hippies&amp;rsquo ; of the great apes , a generally peaceful , matriarchal society that uses sex , not conflict , to resolve disputes . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt;But it became clear to Moore early on that the bonobo world was not as it seemed . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Like many generalizations , the portrayal of bonobos as entirely peaceful is not supported , &amp;rdquo ; she wrote in a blog she posted from the field . &amp;ldquo ; We have witnessed nine encounters between the two groups thus far , and they have ranged from somewhat peaceful events with a lot of sexual behaviour , to extremely aggressive encounters , with bonobos falling from the trees during physical fights and the sounds of bonobo screams filling the forest . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; The Primates paper , written with co-authors Nahoko Tokuyama , Kirsty Graham , Albert Lokasola and Takeshi Furuichi , backs that up . They observed the cannibalism while tracking the bonobos on their day-long rambles through the forests . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; In each of the cannibalism cases , mothers were observed carrying their dead infants for several days , eating parts of the body and in some instances , sharing the meat with another child or another adult female . And the researchers saw lots of bonobo sex , too , particularly by one female named Hide &amp;mdash ; enough that might keep the October issue of Primates wrapped in brown paper on the top shelf at Chapters . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Hide did not exhibit any unusual behaviour while carrying the dead infant , except that she persistently swatted flies that gathered around the carcass , &amp;rdquo ; they wrote . &amp;ldquo ; She traveled with other party members , and engaged in genito-genital rubbing with another female &amp;hellip ; &amp;rdquo ; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; And : &amp;ldquo ; On March 16 , only five days after the cannibalism , Hide&amp;rsquo ; s genitals reached maximal swelling and she started to copulate. &amp;rdquo ; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Though cannibalism isn&amp;rsquo ; t unheard of among the great apes , it usually occurs when the animals are under great stress or during food shortages . The researchers theorize that the mothers carry the dead infants as a form of grieving and that eating the carcass might provide nutrients that improve their chance of reproduction . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Regardless of the reason , seeing cannibalism among the bonobo wasn&amp;rsquo ; t something Moore was expecting , her mother said . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;ldquo ; She was very surprised . It means , he argues , that there are no immutable lessons to be drawn from the Holocaust since its meaning is not fixed . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; He contends that professional historians are much less likely to formulate lessons from the past than polemicists and politicians who often use history to support ideologically driven positions . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Professional historians no longer talk , as they once did , about the lessons of the French Revolution , or the lessons of the fall of the Roman Empire , or even the lessons of Canadian Confederation , &amp;rdquo ; Marrus says . &amp;ldquo ; But if you type &amp;lsquo ; lessons of the Holocaust&amp;rsquo ; into Google , you&amp;rsquo ; ll get millions of hits . But what are these lessons ?
