It&amp;rsquo ; s a series we call the Science of Summer . Today he looks at an environmental disaster that is slowly turning into a victory . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; I was in school back in 1974 when two California scientists published a study with the prosaic title &amp;quot ; Stratospheric sink for chlorofluoromethanes. &amp;quot ; Sherwood Rowland and Mario Molina had discovered that the upper atmosphere is where this class of industrial gases ( and a related group called chlorofluorocarbons , or CFCs ) goes to die , and this rewrote our understanding of how air works . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; It was revolutionary stuff . For the first time , we knew that the structure of our atmosphere itself was vulnerable . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; CFCs were used everywhere in refrigerators , air conditioners and spray cans . The industrial gas had replaced ammonia in fridges because while ammonia cools well ( it&amp;rsquo ; s still used on the International Space Station ) it can leak out and kill people . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; CFCs are harmless at ground level . But not , as it turned out , to the ozone layer in the stratosphere , where the chlorine-based molecules break apart one ozone molecule , move to the next , break it apart too , and keep going for years . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; The ozone layer makes life on land possible by filtering out some of the sun&amp;rsquo ; s UV radiation . And when the Antarctic ozone hole appeared , there was a sense that we were in deep trouble and did n't know what to do about it . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Except we did . The Montreal Protocol of 1987 was a promise signed by most of the world&amp;rsquo ; s countries to stop using CFCs , and the amazing thing is that the signatories kept their promises . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Spray cans went first , mostly even before the ban . Refrigerants went later , but today&amp;rsquo ; s fridges and the AC in your car are free of CFCs . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; But was it too late ? Once you make a part of Earth&amp;rsquo ; s atmosphere go away , can you ever get it back ? &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; This summer brings a happy answer , from one of the foremost ozone scientists in the world , Susan Solomon of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; There wasn&amp;rsquo ; t a lot of attention paid when she published her latest work in the journal Science in early July . But she found the &amp;ldquo ; first signs of healing&amp;rdquo ; in the biggest ozone hole , the one over Antarctica . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; The Antarctic hole forms because of conditions down there . Ozone destruction happens at the fastest rate in deep cold where there is also sunlight . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Late in the Antarctic winter , in August , the sun returns and the southern continent 's air is still at its coldest . The result is a rush of ozone destruction , and the hole grows through September and reaches its peak in October . It can be half the size of the lower 48 U.S. states . &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; Solomon has found that in recent years , the September growth of the hole is not as great as it used to be . The hole is still there , but it&amp;rsquo ; s not the monster it was . It has in fact shrunk by more than four million square kilometres since 2000. &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; I like how she explained it to reporters : &amp;quot ; We can now be confident that the things we 've done have put the planet on a path to heal . Which is pretty good for us , is n't it ? &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; &amp;quot ; Are n't we amazing humans , that we did something that created a situation that we decided collectively , as a world , ' Let 's get rid of these molecules ' ? We got rid of them , and now we 're seeing the planet respond . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;br /&gt; &lt;br /&gt; The significance goes beyond our best defence against ultraviolet light . There is a common belief that humans will destroy the planet and that there is nothing we can do , or will voluntarily do , to prevent this . @@51910552 <h> The Siege of PEI <h> By Moira Welsh -- Investigative Reporter June 13 , 2019 <p> Most islands , Fenech says , have a base of granite or another hard rock . " We do n't have that here , " he says . <p> Bit by bit , Prince Edward Island , made of sandstone and sand , is slowly washing into the sea and " everybody knows it , " Fenech says . <p> As director of the University of PEI Climate Lab , Fenech gives speeches about erosion all over the island . Today , he sits in a homestyle restaurant called Our Family Traditions , with salt fish and deep-fried clams on the menu . Fenech drinks coffee . <p> Erosion is natural . Historical . What 's different now , he says , is the ocean . Water levels are rising . So are ocean temperatures . Their extra heat can add fuel to storms , creating powerful , surging waves that smash against the coast and rip it away . <h> Related Story <p> Winter ice used to appear on the coast in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the shoreline . The sea ice came this year , Fenech says , but over the previous few winters it was hard to find . It used to form along the beaches or the base of soaring red cliffs , growing thick , extending into the ocean so that when a storm came the ice took the brunt of its energy , not the sandstone . <p> Fenech says P.E.I is losing an average of 28 centimetres of land every year . That shoreline often falls off in large chunks in vulnerable locations . There have been some areas where land actually increased , due to shifting sands , but the dominant theme is loss . <p> The UPEI Climate Lab examined infrastructure at risk of damage , or disappearing , due to erosion over the next 90 years . It found 1,000 existing homes , eight barns , seven gazebos , 42 garages , 17 lighthouses , 146 commercial buildings , 50 kilometres of roads and one wind turbine were vulnerable . <p> P.E.I. properties located close to shore are at risk of damage from erosion . But the United Nations suggests Canada needs to cut emissions even more to prevent the worst climate-change impacts . <p> The scientists briefing journalists on the new report acknowledged the emissions cuts need to be global but also said cuts anywhere can have an impact on climate everywhere . <p> The report makes clear that the climate impacts we 're already seeing are going to stay with us for " centuries to millennia " even if we hit the emissions cuts believed necessary to slow warming to a more manageable pace . <p> Bush said , however , there are two vastly different pictures for Canada depending on @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ emissions to zero by 2050 . <p> The report shows if the world can do that , the average temperature increases in Canada by the end of the century will be less than 3 C even in the hardest-hit parts of the country . <p> But if the world keeps emitting at the same rate , most parts of Canada will see increases of between 7 C and 9 C , with the far reaches of the Arctic seeing temperature changes in excess of 11 C. <p> " We are kind of at this fork in the road , " said Chris Derksen , an Environment Canada research scientist specializing in ice cover . These projects will strengthen the development of new tools to help provide maximum value from research investments in genomics and related fields -- areas that produce a massive and ongoing influx of data . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Andrew McArthur , who is a co-leader on two B/CB projects looking to develop new software and database tools that will empower public health agencies and the agri-food sector to more rapidly respond to threats posed by infectious disease outbreaks such as , food-borne illnesses or the growing crisis of microbes resistant to antimicrobials . Kirsty Duncan , Minister of Science <p> " Bioinformatics and Computational Biology is a priority area for Genome Canada given the growing need for enhanced tools and methodologies to make sense of the huge and growing influx of data stemming from genomics research . These tools will change the way we interpret , store , share and use big data , in a cost-effective way . " -- Dr. Paul Lasko , Scientific Director , Institute of Genetics , CIHR <p> Genome Canada is a not-for-profit organization that acts as a catalyst for developing and applying genomics and genomic-based technologies , to create economic and social benefits for Canadians . Genome Canada connects ideas and people across public and private sectors to find new uses for genomics , invests in large-scale science and technology to fuel innovation , and translates discoveries into applications and solutions across key sectors of national importance , including health , agriculture , forestry , fisheries &amp; aquaculture , energy , mining , and the environment . <p> The Canadian Institutes of Health Research(CIHR) is the Government of Canada 's health research investment agency . @@51911243 <h> Why we need a pan-Canadian student nutrition program <p> Kirsty Duncan is a Liberal member of parliament ( Etobicoke North ) and critic for the Environment . She has a Ph.D . in geography ( University of Edinburgh , 1992 ) and has taught meteorology , climatology , and climate change at the University of Windsor , corporate social responsibility and medical geography at the University of Toronto and global environmental processes at Royal Roads University . She served on the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change , an organization that won the 2007 Nobel Prize with Al Gore and is the author of Hunting the 1918 Flu : One Scientist 's Search for a Killer Virus ( University of Toronto Press , 2003 ) , and Environment and Health : Protecting our Common Future ( 2008 ) . <p> Canadian children returned to school this month , and many of them returned hungry ; 40 percent of elementary students and 62 percent of secondary school students do not eat a nutritious breakfast . Poor nutrition status leads to poor health outcomes for children , and Canadian children from all @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ one in five Canadian children who lives below the poverty line . <p> School nutrition programs are highly effective in providing children with nutritious diets . Research confirms the importance of such programs for those who participate , including better grades and health , increased motivation , improved likelihood of graduation , and decreased absenteeism and violence . <p> Despite the clear benefits , Canada remains the only G8 country without a national nutrition program . The 10-15 percent of nutrition programs that do exist survive because administrators and volunteers who operate them are convinced of the benefits . <p> The Conservative government shows no sign of changing course and improving student nutrition . Minister of Health Leona Aglukkaq 's office has said " We see education very clearly as a provincial/territorial jurisdiction , so it 's nothing that 's being considered by our government at this point in time . " This is extremely disappointing considering the recognition by Dr. David Butler-Jones , Chief Public Health Officer of Canada , who has stressed : " As a result of being hungry at school ... children may not reach their @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ health impact throughout their entire lives " . <p> The Minister of Health 's spokesman 's comment is meant to mislead Canadians . Better eating is not only about education , but rather , improving nutrition , grades , and health . Schools are merely the delivery mechanism , as this is where children and youth congregate . This is precisely the reason why , for example , the federal government gives money to the provinces and territories to deliver vaccine programs through schools . <p> If the Minister of Health does not speak for the health of children and youth , who gives a voice to the voiceless , and ensures that every child matters ? This is why we so desperately need a Children 's Commissioner in Canada ( as MP Marc Garneau is advocating ) , who is independent , and who can speak for the most vulnerable in society . The 2009 OECD report , " Doing Better for Children " , provides data on how much each country spends from government funding on children from birth to age 18 . Why were no data available @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Article 12 of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child states : " Children have the right to say what they think should happen when adults are making decisions that affect them , and to have their opinions taken into account . " Our children and youth want to be asked , listened to , heard and respected ; and they want security , including access to safe and healthy food . What is the government 's position in ensuring that children and youth are seriously engaged in making decisions about their lives , especially on something as basic as access to food ? <p> If the government refuses to listen to our young people , perhaps it will listen to the economic argument for a pan-Canadian nutrition program . Recent research from the Toronto District School Board shows that high-school students who eat breakfast before or at school are more likely to graduate than those who do not . <p> The Boston Consulting Group reports that , on average , each high-school graduate contributes an extra $75,000 to the economy . They earn higher salaries than @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ healthcare costs , and are less dependent on social assistance . <p> If providing food at school increases graduation rates by only three percent , a pan-Canadian school meals program in high schools at a cost of $1.25 a day could result in an annual net payback of more than $500 million . <p> The potential economic stimulus for Canadian agriculture is also considerable . Realistically , seventy percent of a pan-Canadian nutrition program could have domestic content with an annual return to Canadian producers of $1.5 billion . As a general rule , for each dollar spent in a community , an additional two to three dollars would be generated through processing , storage , trucking , etc .. <p> Outside North America , school meals are considered an investment rather than a cost . In Sweden , children aged six to 16 receive a hot meal each day by law ; and in Japan , children aged six to 15 receive school meals , with 50 percent of the meals made with local ingredients . <p> In closing , I believe we need concerted and effective advocacy for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ adequate and safe food , which is a right of every individual . This means , first and foremost , listening to the voice of the child . Not one ever chooses or wants to go hungry . <p> The views , opinions and positions expressed by all iPolitics columnists and contributors are the author 's alone . They do not inherently or expressly reflect the views , opinions and/or positions of iPolitics . <h> More from iPolitics <p> X <h> Join the conversation . This initiative will reduce emissions by planting 300 new hectares of trees over three years at the City 's successful willow plantation . <p> Over the lifetime of this project , the City of Calgary will see a cumulative reduction of about 200,000 tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions -- equivalent to removing approximately 61,000 cars off @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ use municipal biosolids as fertilizer and will help create a carbon-storage sink that leads to fewer greenhouse gas emissions . <p> This funding comes from the Champions stream of the Government of Canada 's Low Carbon Economy Challenge , which invests in projects that reduce carbon pollution , save money , and create good jobs . <p> Canada 's climate plan is on track to deliver the largest emissions reduction in the country 's history . @@51911522 <h> The End of the Oil Age Is Upon Us <p> The oil industry is on the cusp of a process of almost total decimation that will begin over the next 30 years , and continue through to the next century . That 's the stark implication of a new forecast by a team of energy analysts led by a former US government energy advisor , seen exclusively by Motherboard . <p> 2020 , the forecast suggests , will go down in history as the final point-of-no-return for the global oil industry -- a date to which we will look back and remember how the production of oil , as well as other fossil fuels like gas and coal , underwent a slow , but inexorable and largely irreversible decline . <p> Along the way , some 80 percent of the industry as we know it is going to be wiped out . <p> Of course , the COVID-19 pandemic is likely to be recognized as a principal trigger for this decline . The new era of oscillating social distancing rules and remote working has crushed once rocketing demand , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ broad contours of this decline were already set in motion even before the pandemic hit . And the implications are stark : we are in the midst of a fundamental energy transition which will see the bulk of the fossil fuel industry gradually eclipsed in coming decades . <p> The end of the line <p> These conclusions are laid out in a soon-to-be-published analysis written by a former top strategy advisor to the US Department of Energy , Rodrigo Villamizar Alvargonz ? lez -- previously Columbian Minister of Energy , World Bank senior economic consultant , an advisor to the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs , and energy expert for the Texas State Senate Economic Development Committee and Texas Public Utility Commission . <p> I obtained the draft manuscript , titled Energy and Power Futures , from the authors earlier this year when it was first finalized in January -- just before the COVID-19 pandemic came on the scene . Villamizar 's forecast placed " the start date of oil 's decline at around 2020 " -- described as a " tipping point " for world oil production which , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ sight is the possibility of going over the all-time production high of 35.7 billion barrels per year ( or 100 million barrels per day ) beyond 2020 . " <p> Villamizar is currently Head of Strategy for the Americas at Kaiserwetter Energy Asset Management , an energy investment firm based in Hamburg , Madrid , and New York . His analysis is co-authored with Randy Willoughby , a professor of political science at San Diego University , and Vicente Lopez-Ibor Mayor , previously founding Chairman of Europe 's largest solar energy company Lightsource BP ( owned by oil and gas giant BP ) and a former Commissioner at Spain 's National Energy Commission . Their study is due to be published later this year by Durham University 's School of Government and International Affairs . <p> After the COVID-19 crisis , they revised their forecasts -- finding that the pandemic has reinforced the trends they had previously identified . In their updated text , they argue that the remaining years of the 21st century and beyond will be marked by a " slow but permanent decline in demand for plenty @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in broad agreement with the predictions of several other agencies , including the Norwegian energy consultancy DNV GL , the US financial consultancy McKinsey , and even oil and gas giant BP , which similarly portend a relentless decline in oil demand out to 2050 . <p> But unlike those predictions , the forecast shows this decline could be faster , with huge ramifications for global oil production . <p> Too much oil ? <p> In the view of Villamizar , Willoughby and Mayor , this is not an oil scarcity crisis , but a demand crisis . They write : " Perhaps we were the first to notice that , even before COVID-19 , the year 2019 would be the last ever to register daily production of oil closer to 100 million barrels . Indeed , before the coronavirus landed in Italy , the size of the oil market had already started its permanent slippery downward slide towards an uncertain future . " <p> In this analysis , oil demand was seen to peak at the end of 2019 and early 2020 . " I thought we had a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " But all the revisions pointed to a similar result . " <p> Among the factors behind the portended decline are a combination of " climate change action initiatives " demanding a brake on fossil fuel production ; a shift toward more electric cars and other forms of transport ; the persistence of lower oil prices undermining oil industry profitability ; and a decrease in investment in new oil infrastructure and technology : <p> " Our results showed petroleum consumption reduced 31 percent by 2050 and 60 percent by 2100 . That means that 2019 was the highest ever production level reached ( 100 million barrels per day , mbd ) . " <p> Villamizar and his colleagues point out that oil will still be needed for many key industries , including petrochemicals and plastics . <p> And there are vast reserves of oil still in the ground . So the industry will not simply disappear . But most of the world 's oil assets will , in their view , become ' stranded ' -- left alone because global demand for it gradually evaporates . <p> The overall prognosis @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ final half of the oil age -- is sobering : " Oil will not die anytime soon but it is already on a downward slippery slope . " <p> Natural selection <p> While the oil industry as such will not simply collapse , these experts believe it is now entering a protracted period of terminal decline over the next three decades . What emerges as a consequence will be a very different type of industry . <p> " We forecast a long-term Darwinian transformation in the future oil sector , " write Villamizar , Willoughby , and Mayor . " The new market structure rising from the old oil reality will be dominated by an oil troika made up of US , Saudi Arabia , and Russia . " <p> Only 20 percent of industry players will survive by 2050 , they forecast . And the oil market will be " one-third smaller than today . " <p> This drop in demand means , of course , that global oil production will also decline because it is no longer needed . According to the authors , production will decline from @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ mbd by mid-century , and 40 mbd by 2100 . <p> The world will simultaneously see a dramatic reduction of exports from 46 mbd to about 25 mbd by 2050 , and a reduction in the number of exporting countries from today 's 58 to about 15 . <p> These projected declines in global oil production by a third , and in global oil exports by nearly half -- within the next 30 years -- comprises a colossal collapse by any standard . <p> The analysts compare this sweeping oil sector transformation to the decimation of the tobacco industry . This time , the result will be " fewer players , shrinking markets and lots of enemies everywhere accusing the companies of selling an environmentally poisonous product ... With less water in a shrinking pond , the bigger fish will push the smaller out and regroup in isolated sections of what 's left . " <p> Climate danger <p> But it is too early to rejoice that the coming decimation of the oil industry will happen sufficiently fast to save us from dangerous climate change . <p> Villamizar , Willoughby @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ level of oil supply is still much higher than what the Paris Agreement on climate mitigation expects to be produced to maintain the world 's average temperature above no higher than 2 degree Celsius from the level registered during the Industrial Revolution . " <p> So it would be a huge mistake to sit back and wait casually for the oil industry to slowly die out . That approach would put us on a path to breach the scientifically recognized 2C safe limit . Beyond that level , scientists warn that we will experience an increasingly deadly and unpredictable climate . <p> And some scientists warn that even now , due to the uncertainties in predicting how tightly interconnected complex ecosystems might unfold , we may already be on the brink of triggering a runaway warming process that could culminate in an uninhabitable planet . <p> This predicament puts the task of rapidly decarbonizing our economy at the forefront of global priorities . That will , according to Villamizar and his co-authors , require huge investments in " areas like electrification , affordable long-term energy storage , and regenerative agriculture @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ mindsets , and thus a shift to a slower but perhaps more stable economy -- instead of expecting quick bucks for the next quarter , investors should recognize the need to wait 10-15 years for returns , they argue . <p> Supply or demand ? <p> While the demand slump is right now the big factor in the global oil crisis , several other studies have pointed out that the oil industry was overdue a reckoning due to the increasing costs of oil production and how this might impact supply relative to profits . <p> Earlier in February , I reported on a major study by the Geological Survey of Finland which assessed the implications of the fact that conventional oil production began to plateau around 2005 . After this point , the world has become increasingly dependent on unconventional oil and gas supplies . Since 2008 , the rise in demand has been met almost entirely by more expensive and difficult to extract sources such as shale oil , tar sands and offshore drilling . <p> While market prices have remained too low for oil companies to make a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ they have ramped up billions of dollars in debt to keep the show on the road : all enabled by massive post-2008 quantitative easing . Thus , the study warned : <p> " The era of cheap and abundant energy is long gone . Money supply and debt have grown faster than the real economy . Debt saturation and paralysis is now a very real risk , requiring a global scale reset . " <p> In June , a peer-reviewed study led by Dr Roger Bentley of the Petroleum Analysis Centre in Ireland found that global conventional oil production had indeed reached a " resource-limited plateau " from 2005 onwards . Although this was relieved by the rise in US shale oil , even before the pandemic there were signs that the shale boom " may be fairly short-lived . " <p> The new forecast from Villamizar and his co-authors , when taken into context with such studies , suggests that the oil industry now faces a perfect storm of crises affecting both supply and demand . <p> Production was increasingly uneconomical due to the transition to more expensive and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ debt-drenched economics of unconventional resources mean that , however vast those reserves are , it was increasingly unviable to continue extraction without even more unsustainable levels of debt . Meanwhile , global demand was already set to begin a slow but precipitous decline from 2020 onwards . But the pandemic accelerated that collapse in demand , and we have reached the point-of-no-return . <p> If this analysis is right , then the end of the oil age is in full swing . The real question is , how fast can we transition to what comes next ? <p> Russia declared a state of emergency after a power plant spilled 20,000 metric tons of oil and diesel fuel into a river in the Arctic Circle . The possible cause : melting permafrost due to climate change .

The Government of Canada has invested close to $10 million so that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ iconic site . <p> The Chambly Jetty ( also known as the Federal Wharf ) is located in the heart of Old Chambly , downstream from Lock No. 1 in the Chambly Basin . The new facilities ensure user safety and maintain the recreational activities associated with the Canal . New street furniture has also been added to make the visitor experience even more enjoyable . <p> The Chambly Canal is a true oasis for cycling , boating and outdoor enthusiasts and offers moments of total relaxation in a place shaped by 175 years of history . In addition , its nine locks , as well as one bridge , are now manually operated by lock operators , just as they were when the Canal opened in 1843 . <p> In recent years , the Chambly Canal National Historic Site has undergone a major facelift , including infrastructure projects at the Chambly Jetty and the restoration of locks numbers 1 , 2 , 3 and 9 in Chambly and Saint-Jean-sur-Richelieu . This is an enormous boost for tourism and the many jobs that depend on it . " <p> The Honorable Pablo Rodriguez Quebec Lieutenant and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons <h> Quick facts <p> Built in the early 1840s , the structure of the Chambly Jetty has been modified several times to date . The Chambly Jetty is an important cultural resource at the Chambly Canal National Historic Site . Along with the historic cabins , the Superintendent 's house is one of the main elements of the northern entrance to this important navigation corridor on the Richelieu River . <p> Following the flooding of the Richelieu River in 2011 , the Chambly Jetty was closed to ensure user safety . Rehabilitation work took place over 18 months , starting in the fall of 2018 . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ work at the Chambly Canal National Historic Site as part of the largest federal infrastructure plan in the history of Parks Canada . This investment will help ensure these treasured places are protected and preserved in the future .

's carbon tax applies a single price to the province 's fossil-fuel-originated CO2 emissions : It started at $10/tonne in July 2008 and has moved @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ July 2012 , it will hit $30/tonne . Exempted processes , including natural gas flaring , mean that about 25 per cent of B.C. 's CO2 emissions are untaxed . <p> More than a tax , B.C. has imposed a tax shift : The money collected from the carbon tax pushes personal and corporate taxes down , while steadily ramping up taxes on fossil fuels . Over time , this continually rising price provides an incentive for people and businesses to use less and find alternatives : Anyone who can lower their fuel usage and/or energy consumption , pays less tax . -- C.P. <p> Such cautionary tales make British Columbia 's carbon pricing experiment all the more remarkable ( see sidebar for the elements ) . There are a dozen or so carbon taxes in the world today ( a chart laying all of them out can be found on page 16 of this report ) . Of all those levies , enacted by a patchwork of nations , provinces and even municipalities ( Boulder , Colo. , has one ) , B.C. 's tax has been widely hailed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ We Have a Winner : British Columbia 's Carbon Tax Woos Sceptics , gushed one headline in the Economist in July , as did a similarly glowing feature earlier this year in the New York Times , which suggested a B.C.-styled carbon tax could solve America 's debt woes . <p> Yet in British Columbia today many remain less than enthused . Social advocates say the poor are being squeezed too hard by the tax , while an unfair chunk of the revenue is being given back to corporations . Environmentalists warn that the tax , which rose to $25/tonne on July 1 , is too slight to change our bad energy habits . Meanwhile business leaders insist our small , resource-based economy should n't " dance alone " while global competitors continue to pollute unhindered . <p> Already one potential future premier , John Cummins of the upstart BC Conservatives , is proposing to kill the carbon tax , apparently believing the public mood has changed since then-NDP leader Carole James campaigned in 2008 on a promise to " axe the tax " -- and handed the BC Liberals @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of B.C. 's carbon tax experiment uncertain , and the next provincial election looming in May 2013 , now may be the time for a little sober reflection : What has the B.C. carbon tax really achieved so far ? What can we expect to see if we stick with the tax ? And how might it need to change ? <p> Good news for a change <p> One who calls our carbon tax a good-news story , is Stewart Elgie , a University of Ottawa law and economics professor and chair of the green economy think-tank Sustainable Prosperity . <p> Elgie says B.C. 's gasoline consumption has dropped by three per cent compared to the rest of Canada since the introduction of the tax , an effect that can not be attributed to the post-2008 recession . He also points out that B.C. 's GDP has grown slightly in the three years since the tax appeared -- indicating at a bare minimum that the carbon tax has n't hurt the economy . That , says Elgie , is because B.C. 's tax on fossil fuels was designed from the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ revenue neutral " -- most of the money it collects from taxpayers is given back in the form of lower income and corporate taxes . <p> And while the carbon tax might not have won the last election for the Liberals , it did n't lose it for them either . ( Politicians both inside and outside B.C. take note -- recent polling for the Pembina Institute shows that public support for the carbon tax remains strong ; strong for a tax , at least . ) <p> " B.C. is now the lowest per-capita gasoline user in Canada , and also has the lowest income tax rates in Canada , " says Elgie . " That is in large part because of the carbon tax shift . " <p> In 2008 , B.C. emitted 68.7 million tonnes ( Mt ) of greenhouse gas emissions , measured in carbon dioxide equivalent ( CO2e ) . In all of 2009 , total greenhouse gas emissions in British Columbia were down slightly to 66.9 megatonnes CO2e , according to the provincial government . Updated stats for 2010 will not be published until @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ? <p> It 's still early days for the B.C. tax . What can we expect in the years to come ? It helps to look at Sweden , where a carbon tax has been in place for 20 years . <p> In 1991 , Sweden imposed a carbon tax of just over $50/tonne of CO2 . By December of 2008 , greenhouse emissions had dropped by more than 40 per cent from levels of the mid-1970s -- well below its Kyoto commitments -- as Swedes embraced renewable energy from biomass , heat pumps and waste heat recovery , and expanded their use of district heating systems . <p> In 2008 , Swedish Environment Minister Andreas Carlgren credited Sweden 's tax policy for cutting its emissions by 20 per cent below what levels would have been without it . " A carbon tax , " Calgren told the Guardian at the time , " is the most cost-effective way to make carbon cuts , and it does not prevent strong economic growth . " <p> The Swedish carbon tax is not identical to ours . Most prominently , it is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ about twice the dollar-per-tonne rate that ours reached only this year , and the top rate has jumped to about $100 per metric tonne since its inception . On the other hand , many Swedish industries pay a lower rate ( about $22/tonne ) , not all fossil fuels are covered , and proceeds go into general government revenues instead of tax cuts . <p> But the similarities between Sweden and B.C. are nonetheless striking . Both have a small population , widely dispersed across a forested , northern land base with just a few large cities . Both rely on a lot of hydro for electricity . <p> " When you look at B.C. 's policies , " says Mark Jaccard , an environmental economist at Simon Fraser University , " you see the very same things we saw in the first years of the Swedish policy , which is the beginning of this disconnect between economic output and emissions . " <p> Elgie finds that pattern repeated across the handful of other European countries -- including Finland and the Netherlands -- that have followed the carbon tax path @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ society begins to alter its behaviour and infrastructure in response to the higher prices . During this early phase , as in B.C. , critics insist the tax is not working . <p> But , as Elgie points out , no one buys a new car or modernizes their factory every month . Yet if you know the price of energy will keep going up over time , fuel efficiency becomes a prime consideration the next time such an investment needs to be made . <p> The experience of others shows that 15 years on , carbon emissions can go down by five or six per cent with no negative impact on GDP . " The story we 're seeing in B.C. is pretty much the same story that 's already played out in countries with more experience , " says Elgie . " Good for the environment , no harm to the economy . " <p> Tweak the tax ? <p> That 's not to say B.C. 's carbon tax could n't be made better , even in the eyes of admirers . It covers only about 75 per @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . The rest , such as flaring from gas wells or non-combustion processes in cement and aluminum manufacturing , remain untaxed . " Let 's go after that final 25 per cent , " urges Mark Jaccard . <p> In particular , Jaccard fingers natural gas production as a growing emission source that could " swamp all of our efforts , " unless we take action . " Tell them they ca n't emit ( greenhouse gases ) into the air , end of story , " he says . <p> But gas facilities are n't the only places where emissions " leak " past B.C. 's tax : landfills , smelters and cement kilns are others . Jaccard 's view ? " Regulate everybody . Tell them they 'll have to measure what is coming out . And , we 're taxing you on it . " Jaccard says this hard line could be phased in , however , to allow companies and regional districts time to prepare . <p> If that seems radical , note that such an approach has been taken before in B.C. In early 2007 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ two coal-fuelled plants -- until premier Gordon Campbell decreed that all future sources of electricity must be zero-emission . The projects were promptly cancelled . <p> B.C. Minister of Environment Terry Lake agrees that industrial emissions should not be exempt from carbon pricing . " There are ways to capture those fugitive emissions and I quite agree that we should , " he told the Tyee . " If we did n't want to go with cap and trade , we certainly could expand the carbon tax to capture those non-combustible emissions as well . " <p> " Devil in the details " <p> Marc Lee , an economist with the Canadian Centre For Policy Alternatives , gives Gordon Campbell credit for bringing in " a policy industry did not want . " But while other pundits laud B.C. 's carbon tax shift , Lee is underwhelmed . He does n't buy Elgie 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a tonne , the carbon tax is too small to have ( created ) any change in behaviour , even now that we 're in the fourth year , " Lee says . Any tax that makes fossil fuels more expensive is technically a carbon tax , sending a price signal to consumers and business to use less . He cites Ontario 's application of the HST to gasoline and diesel as an example . Raising the tax in July 2010 from five per cent ( under GST ) to 13 per cent ( with HST ) created a higher tax on the carbon in a litre of motor fuel than our own B.C. carbon tax . <p> And in a report published in February , Lee points out that B.C. @@51912123 <h> A failure of the brain 's reward circuits may lead to anhedonia . <h> THE BASICS <p> Anhedonia is one of the main symptoms of major depressive disorder ( MDD ) . It is the loss of interest in previously rewarding or enjoyable activities . People suffering from clinical depression lose interest in hobbies , friends , work , and even food and sex . It 's as if the brain 's pleasure circuits shut down or short out . But do they ? Some experts define hedonic function as the total amount of pleasure that it 's possible to gain from a single activity . Perhaps depression reduces that hedonic capacity . Certainly , as I report in Brain Sense , we know that the brain 's pleasure circuits can be modified -- for example from a deep aversion to salty taste to a real orgasm of salt pleasure . <p> But depression may not shut down pleasure circuits entirely . An alternative theory suggests that anhedonia comes not from a reduced capacity to experience pleasure , but instead from an inability to sustain good feelings over time @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , but only briefly -- not long enough to sustain interest or involvement in life 's good things . <p> How can you find out the difference ? When it comes to pleasure pathways , the brain 's geographic layout is complex . Areas associated with reward and motivation include the nucleus accumbens ( or NA , deep inside the " primitive brain " ) ; and higher up , the prefrontal cortex ( or PFC , the thin outer layer of the brain behind the forehead ) . It 's likely that nerve impulses travel in both directions to maintain reward and motivation . That is , " feel good " signals travel upward to the PFC , but nerve fibers from the PFC also send signals down to the NA . Some evidence suggests that , in normal brains , signals traveling downward from the PFC to the NA may sustain interest in a pleasurable activity . If that 's true , then the depressed brain might have trouble using the PFC to sustain NA activity over time . <p> Today , Aaron Heller and his colleagues at @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ UK ) published a paper that sheds some light on that hypothesis . They report in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences on their new functional magnetic resonance imaging ( fMRI ) studies of brain activation patterns in depressed and nondepressed people . The people looked at pleasant , unpleasant , and neutral pictures over a 37-minute period , but the volunteers were n't passive . They made a conscious effort to enhance the mood the picture produced , whether happy , sad , or indifferent . The study delivered five important insights : <p> In response to positive images , the depressed brains did n't sustain NA activation as well as the normal brains did -- no matter how hard they tried . <p> Difficulties sustaining activity in the NA were associated with reduced activity in the PFC . <p> Those depressed subjects who were better able to sustain NA activity also reported higher levels of positive emotion in their everyday lives . <p> The deficit in sustaining NA activity was specific to positive emotion . ( Apparently , happiness is hard to sustain but sadness is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ) <p> If you are depressed and suffering from anhedonia , you 're probably asking , " So what ? " How does knowing what 's going on in the brain offer hope to individuals trapped in despair ? I think it 's important for at least two reasons . Pure scientific research gets to the heart of " how things work . " If we can understand what goes wrong in anhedonia , we may be able to develop drugs or behavioral therapies that coax the PFC into reinstating its sustained activation of the NA . This research also provides a new way to measure whether experimental treatments work . And those possibilities for treatment and assessment -- admittedly for the future -- should cheer even the most stubborn anhedonia . <p> I have anhedonia , I have had it for a year and 2 months now , i am on antispsychotic medications and i just hope that they are to blame , because its one of the worst illnesses i can imagine having . @@51912179 <h> Welfare of Polar Bears <p> Conservation Coordinator Dylan McCart is with PhD student Stephanie Penk developing a method to measure polar bears that is voluntary for the bear . Photo provided by the Polar Bear Habitat.TP.jpegjpeg , TP <p> Tourism has been slowly ramping up at the Habitat since we reopened on July 1 , with some days looking almost like a typical summer day -- besides the masks , sanitizer , and social distancing , of course . <p> We have been fortunate to be able to welcome some of our volunteers back to the Habitat , too . We are up to four dedicated people helping out to prepare the bear diets on a weekly basis , and we are so grateful for their valuable contributions . With the hot temperatures , the bears have been spending plenty of time in the water . Each enclosure has at least one water source at all times , and of course the bears always have access to indoor air-conditioned rooms , too . <p> Eddy in particular has developed a habit of laying in the shallow waters of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ on end . He will be able to continue this favourite activity for the rest of the summer , as his return home to the Quebec Aquarium has once again been delayed due to construction . <p> Dylan McCart , the Habitat 's Conservation Coordinator , was recently featured by the International Association for Bear Research and Management ( IBA ) for his Masters study , which is looking at the hormone patterns of male polar bears in different social conditions . With help from a grant from the IBA , he is investigating whether testosterone levels in males differ in the presence and absence of females . The results could improve the housing conditions for all polar bears in human care . <p> Another study , published in Nature Climate Change by respected polar bear scientist Peter Molnar and his team , received a lot of media attention this past month , too . It predicted that polar bears in some regions -- like those closest to Cochrane -- would not have enough resources to be able to reproduce by the end of this decade . One of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ collaborating with the Habitat for data collection related to this body of research . Penk visited the Habitat and worked with our team to develop a new method to measure polar bears . The measurements taken at the Habitat help understand the relationship between a polar bear 's size and his energy needs and will contribute to science 's understanding of polar bear populations in a changing climate . The data collected here are the most consistent and robust in the world -- and it 's all done voluntarily . <p> These are excellent examples of the Habitat 's contribution to the welfare of polar bears and underscore the importance of our incredible facility . Our Board of Directors is continuing to work on securing funding solutions for the Habitat to ensure this important work can continue . Thank you for your ongoing support ! Note : This is a monthly column presented in partnership with the Cochrane Times-Post. 
@@51912192 <h> 2020 Is Proving Another Disastrous Year For Our Earth 's Climate <h> The year already has been marked by rising global temperatures , Arctic ice melts and intensifying wildfires and storms . <p> Record-breaking heat , melting ice caps , raging wildfires and a particularly grim hurricane forecast may have taken a backseat in news cycles dominated by politics and a health pandemic , but that does n't mean these climate phenomena have gone away . <p> The year still has more than four months to go , but 2020 already has proven itself to be another eventful one in terms of natural disasters , rising global temperatures and threatening environmental outlooks . <p> Here 's a look at just some of the anomalies we 've faced so far in 2020 . <p> Sean Gallup via Getty ImagesMountains nearly devoid of snow stand behind a road and a polar bear warning sign during a summer heatwave on Svalbard archipelago on July 29 near Longyearbyen , Norway . <p> During the first seven months of the year , the Earth 's global land and ocean surface temperature set its second-highest @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 14.88 Celsius ) was only .007 of a degree less than the record set in 2016 . <p> July also saw the global temperature rise 1.66 degrees Fahrenheit ( 0.92 of a degree Celcius ) above the 20th-century average , tying it with 2016 as the second-hottest July on record . It was just .02-degree short of 2019 's record rise in July of 1.71-degree Fahrenheit ( 0.95 of a degree Celcius ) . <p> The Northern Hemisphere , meanwhile , saw the highest ever recorded combined land and ocean surface average temperature in July , with the mercury rising 2.12 degrees Fahrenheit ( 1.18 degree Celcius ) above average . This combined temperature surpassed July 2019 by 0.14 of a degree Fahrenheit ( 0.08 of a degree Celcius ) . <p> NOAAGlobal land and ocean temperature anomalies in July . <p> " The six warmest Julys on record have occurred in the last six years , consistent with our warming climate , " NOAA reported . <h> Loss Of Sea Ice <p> Unfortunately , all this heat affects more than just air conditioner sales . <p> July set a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ? 120,000 square miles below the previous record low mark for July set in 2019 , according to the National Snow and Ice Data Center ( NSIDC ) . And the figure for this July was 840,000 square miles below the 1981-2010 average . <p> The ice loss was attributed to above-average air temperatures and extensive melt pond development , which reduces the ice surface 's ability to reflect light and consequently allows more of the sun 's energy to be absorbed , the NSIDC said . <p> The 4,000-year-old Milne Ice Shelf in Nunavut , Canada , lost more than 40% of its area , or 31 square miles , over two days in late July . <p> Canada 's ice shelves were a sheet spanning approximately 3,475-square miles when discovered by polar explorer Robert Peary in 1902 , according to NSIDC.By 2000 , it had been reduced to just 405 square miles , the BBC reported . <p> " This drastic decline in ice shelves is clearly related to climate change , " University of Ottawa glaciology professor Luke Copland said in a statement . " This summer @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Fahrenheit ) warmer than the average over the period from 1981 to 2010 , and the region has been warming at two to three times the global rate . The Milne and other ice shelves in Canada are simply not viable any longer and will disappear in the coming decades . " <p> The St. Patrick Bay ice caps , also in Nunavut , completely vanished last month . The caps were reduced to only five percent of their former area between 1959-2015 and then rapidly deteriorated after an especially warm summer in 2015 , according to NSIDC and NASA imagery . <p> " We 've long known that as climate change takes hold , the effects would be especially pronounced in the Arctic , " said NSIDC Director Mark Serreze , who conducted research on the St. Patrick Bay ice caps as a graduate student in 1982 . The EAC report explains : <p> Trees are frequently cited as the best storm-water management tool because of their ability to slow and filter stormwater runoff . <p> Trees act as natural pollution filters ; <p> Tree roots remove nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus , both by-products of urban living , which can pollute local streams and rivers . These root systems also help to hold the soil in place , decreasing the amount of sediment that enters local streams and rivers ; <p> Homeowners can save up to 58% on daytime air conditioning costs with properly-placed trees ; <p> Trees act as a carbon sink by removing the carbon from carbon dioxide and storing it as cellulose in the trunk while releasing the oxygen back into the air . A healthy tree stores about 13 pounds @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ year ; and <p> Estimates project that trees produce enough oxygen on each acre for 18 people every day , and absorb enough carbon dioxide on each acre , over a year 's time , to equal the amount you produce when you drive your car 26,000 miles . <p> We welcome your feedback and encourage you to share your thoughts . In this sense , the U.S. President 's lineage can be traced through @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Long , through Red-baiting senator Joseph McCarthy in the 1950s , to segregationist governor and presidential candidate George Wallace in the 1960s and 1970s . Indeed , Mr. Trump 's most recent re-election gambit -- representing the forces of " law and order " against urban protesters -- directly swipes from Richard Nixon 's successful 1968 playbook . <p> But in a more fundamental way , Trumpism owes more to P.T. Barnum and Arthur Nielsen than to Ronald Reagan and Barry Goldwater . In fact , his election was more or less the culmination of a 30-year process in which right-wing politics was transformed into a huge and vastly profitable business . <p> The seeds were planted in 1987 , when the Federal Communications Commission ( FCC ) , the U.S. broadcast regulator , eliminated its so-called " fairness doctrine , " which required broadcasters to present contrasting views in any airtime discussions of controversial public issues . That decision opened the way to the first generation of right-wing talk radio -- and stars such as Rush Limbaugh -- and television , particularly Fox News . Over the past 20 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , carried on what radio and television started , catering to a vast audience -- and , equally important , a vast advertising base -- that revels in angry , often apocalyptic , wall-to-wall political indoctrination , packaged as news and performing as entertainment . <p> As the historian Rick Perlstein explained in an influential 2012 essay , The Long Con , this massive politico-entertainment complex has more to do with money than it does to politics . And the profit machine works on the most reliable , time-tested technique of all in mass media : attracting eyeballs and selling advertising , ideally in huge volumes . <p> Consider that , according to Forbes , marquee Fox News host Sean Hannity earned US$36-million in 2018 . It is an endless cycle that radicalizes viewers and monetizes that radicalization -- with the purveyors laughing all the way to the bank . <p> That 's why the Trump phenomenon is n't at play here : the simple demographic reasons of our population size , and as a result , the inability to generate a huge economic payout . <p> Just ask Pierre-Karl P ? ladeau . What 's not comparable : a U.S. viewing audience that is many times larger , and thus infinitely more profitable . <p> Sun News is just the most dramatic example of how Canada 's national makeup and economy of scale protect us from the most noxious manifestations of right-wing politics . @@51915474 <h> DEEP DIVE : The role of geoparks in Canada 's sustainability <p> This brief is one of a series produced by the Building Back Better Post-COVID-19 Task Force , a group of experts and partners affiliated with the Canadian Commission for UNESCO and its UNESCO Chairs Network . Their goal is to bring together sustainable economic recovery ideas to make our communities stronger in a post-COVID-19 world . <p> The series highlights how responding to the COVID-19 crisis through adaptive and strategic infrastructure investments can preserve critical ecosystems , increase the use of green infrastructure , and protect regional resources and distribution systems . These infrastructures can meet basic human needs and improve human health , while fostering long-term community resilience , well-being and sustainable employment . <p> The suggestions offered in this series support Canada 's commitments to the UN Agenda 2030 Sustainable Development Goals and position the country as a world leader in developing new economies based on environmental sustainability . <p> The COVID-19 global public health crisis has affected Canadians on all levels . Yet Canada is a country of resilient people , connected to a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ shaped our ability to withstand the most extreme natural events . Navigating these challenging times and emerging as a thriving nation is consistent with the goals of UNESCO Global Geoparks . Through the five Canadian UNESCO Global Geoparks and six Aspiring Geoparks , there is an occasion to support a range of scientific , cultural , and educational opportunities that stimulate and diversify our economy , enabling us to overcome this unprecedented crisis . <p> UNESCO Global Geoparks are territories with geological heritage and landscapes of international importance connected to an area 's outstanding natural and cultural heritage . Global Geoparks are also innovative in raising awareness of key issues facing society in the context of the natural environment . Through education and local and regional partnerships , they draw attention to the interconnectivity between socio-economic development and the conservation of natural resources . Moreover , thanks to their origins as grassroots , community-driven initiatives , they function as honest brokers in supporting local sustainable development . <p> The Canadian presence is growing on the international stage , and Canada is an emerging leader in Geoparks working with both Indigenous @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ As UNESCO designations , they have a mandate to implement the UN Agenda 2030 Sustainable Development Goals . <p> Earth 's extraordinary place <p> UNESCO Global Geoparks showcase the beauty and diversity of Earth 's extraordinary places , and Canada has immense opportunity to celebrate Earth 's heritage . By promoting education and exploration of these unique territories , local citizens gain pride in their community and connection to the land . Although they showcase local geological heritage , Geoparks are all about local communities . <p> Often located in rural and remote areas with backgrounds in resource development ( such as the coal economy of Tumbler Ridge or the cod fishery off the Discovery Global Geopark 's northeastern coast of Newfoundland ) , Geoparks promote tourism development with a focus on both environmental and economic sustainability , thereby offering opportunities for local communities to diversify their economies . <p> The Perc ? Geopark 's Tektonik Experiential Pavilion was created as the cornerstone of the new UNESCO Global Geopark . Locals and visitors experience hands-on displays demonstrating the interconnectedness of natural and cultural history on the Gasp ? Peninsula . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ investment leading to successful diversification ; since the Geopark 's designation , the region has seen a record increase in visitors and associated local economic prosperity . New tours and outside activities are being offered in 2020 to continue programming safely with COVID-19 restrictions . <p> In the Tumbler Ridge Geopark , the panoramic vistas of the Canadian Rocky Mountains overlook valleys and plains rich with Cretaceous-period dinosaur footprints and fossils , and rich coal deposits . The Geo Interpretive Centre is under development , and ongoing fundraising will revitalize an underused property in the downtown core . Open-air exhibit pods will teach about the connections between the mountains and the ancient sea floor , the dinosaurs , and Indigenous stories of giant trackways , while an espresso and gelato bar around an open gathering space will provide new life and traffic in the downtown . Pop-up market space and an open-air stage encourage future foot traffic , small business growth , and recurring visits to the picturesque town . <p> Territories of resilience <p> UNESCO Global Geoparks are sustainable development territories where their resilience is rooted in their cultural @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ resilient territories respond to disruption and crises by developing innovative solutions through strong collaborative partnerships with local communities . Indigenous peoples have a long and storied history of overcoming overwhelming adversity and systemic injustice . As the current pandemic has permanently altered the economic landscape , Canadian Geoparks , with their meaningful partnerships with local Indigenous communities , are well-positioned to facilitate the transition to a new tourism economy , creating local jobs that preserve and share culture . @@51915581 <h> Seth Klein discusses his new book on tackling the climate crisis like we 've fought wars -- and now the pandemic . <p> Called to the new fight . Image credits : Joseph Sydney Hallam ( left ) ; Meital Smith ( right ) . <p> Seth Klein spends a lot of time thinking about emergencies . Earlier this spring , the former director of the B.C. office of the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives had just finished writing a book drawing lessons for fighting climate change from the country 's Second World War experience when the coronavirus hit . Whether it 's a war against Nazi aggression , a deadly and infectious virus or a climate emergency irreversibly changing our country , collective dangers require swift and transformative action . They are opportunities to overhaul conventional wisdom . <p> In a recent interview with The Tyee about his forthcoming book , which is currently available for pre-order , Klein expands on that argument , explaining how Canada 's $250-billion response to COVID-19 has shattered mainstream conceptions about what 's feasible for climate action . He discusses what the Second World War can teach us about reducing social inequality in the face of a crisis , and the crucial role Indigenous people have played in both our wartime efforts and our current battles on climate change . <p> Geoff Dembicki : Where does the interest in WWII come from ? I 've always been intrigued with what WWII has to tell us about how quickly we can ramp up an economic transformation and retool the economy in the space of a few years . Because I think often people wrestle with this feeling on climate change that the task is so great and there 's so little time , can we really do this ? But the more I delved into history , I kept seeing these parallels with WWII all over the place and not just with respect to the economic transition , but across a whole host of areas . <p> And then right when you were done writing the book , we entered this coronavirus emergency . Almost a third of active farmland in the Vancouver area is leased , and it 's an approach the provincial government has encouraged as it tries to increase the number of young farmers in the province . <p> Between 2011 and 2016 , the average B.C. farmer was 56 years old , and about 3,000 farmers stopped farming . Endowed with economies of scale , these landowners maximize their profits by farming industrially -- an agricultural model that relies on pesticides , fossil fuels , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ markets . <p> Farmland in the Vancouver area costs between $150,000 to $350,000 per acre . That 's more than most B.C. farmers can afford . Most would need to increase their prices by up to 70 per cent if they had to pay off mortgages on agricultural land . <p> In contrast , small farmers like Suda grow several crops on their land in a season , producing more food and money per acre than industrial farms , and with minimal environmental impacts . They also better serve local markets and directly reinvest their profits into the B.C. economy . <p> Close to 70 per cent of the vegetables consumed in B.C. come from large farms in Mexico or California , two regions where agricultural production is anticipated to decline due to climate change and water scarcity . <p> And COVID-19 has made the issue more pressing : California 's Central Valley -- the epicenter of North America 's industrial vegetable production , and a key supplier to B.C. -- has been hit hard by the pandemic . " data-portal-copyright= " Valerie Wutti " **28;11443;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 568214 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Brock Badgers and Saskatchewan Huskies will play for the Canadian university women&amp;rsquo ; s basketball championship on Sunday . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It&amp;rsquo ; s a matchup featuring two schools that between them have a combined total of one previous U Sports title , by the Huskies in 2015. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Badgers earned their right to play for the Bronze Baby Trophy at TD Place arena at 5 p.m. by shutting down the University of Prince Edward Island Panthers 69-55 in one Saturday semifinal , while the Huskies cruised past the Laval Rouge et Or 76-57. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Panthers and Rouge et Or will meet in the bronze-medal game scheduled for 12 noon . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Brock 69 , UPEI 55&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A tight contest through three quarters , with Brock leading just 52-48 , blew open when the Badgers held national player of the year Jenna Mae Elsworth and her Panthers teammates scoreless for the first five minutes of the period . By that time , the Ontario champions were up by 16. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s just incredible . I never really believed or dreamed of this moment , honestly , &amp;rdquo ; said Badgers guard Melissa Tatti , who scored 14 points , &amp;ldquo ; and I wouldn&amp;rsquo ; t rather be with anybody else . My team is amazing , and we are an army . We are literally an army . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We never let down . We play like we&amp;rsquo ; re behind 15 points . Every possession , we give it ( all ) . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Brock forward Samantha Keltos led all scorers with 23 points . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Honestly , when we are up like that , we never think that we are up , &amp;rdquo ; she said . &amp;ldquo ; To us , it&amp;rsquo ; s a close game and anything can happen . We just keep pushing it and keep doing our thing . We just never let up . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Elsworth scored the first seven points of the game for the Panthers and finished with 19 . Reese Baxendale chipped in with 14. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; **26;11473;TOOLONG 76 , Laval 57&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Defence made the difference in this one , too . The Huskies allowed only six points in the first quarter , and a 13-0 run over about 3 1/2 minutes of the second extended their lead to 20. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Laval turned up the pressure to begin the second half and the margin dropped to a dozen , but Saskatchewan was &lt;span style= " font-family : -apple-system , BlinkMacSystemFont , ' Segoe UI ' , Roboto , Oxygen-Sans , Ubuntu , Cantarell , ' Helvetica Neue ' , sans-serif ; " &gt;never really threatened by the prospect of losing . The score was 53-37 through three quarters and the westerners ' advantage quickly jumped to 20 in the fourth . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Megan Ahlstrom topped Saskatchewan with 16 points . Libby Epoch and Kyla Shand both had 12 and Summer Masikewich added 11. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We are really lucky to be here for the third time in the past five years , &amp;rdquo ; Ahlstrom said , &amp;ldquo ; but we are definitely not taking anything for granted because we have business to take care of , and we still have one more game that we are focusing on now . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;11501;TOOLONG ... title= " Gatineau 's Khal ? ann Caron-Goudreau of the Rouge et Or reaches for a rebound in front of Kyla Shand of the Huskies in the first half . Besides that 2015 championship , they were in the 2018 final before losing to the Carleton Ravens and played in last year&amp;rsquo ; s bronze-medal game before losing to the Ottawa Gee-Gees. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The way I see Brock playing is that they&amp;rsquo ; re just fearless , &amp;rdquo ; Huskies head coach Lisa Thomaidis said . &amp;ldquo ; They don&amp;rsquo ; t seem to be playing with any pressure at all and just doing their thing . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; For us , I think it helps us as far as having experience . Ravens march on at men 's basketball nationals , downing Dinoshttp : **35;12290;TOOLONG ... src= " https : **34;12327;TOOLONG ... title= " Alain Louis of the Carleton Ravens goes to the basket against Ezeoha Santiago of the Calgary Dinos in a men 's quarterfinal of the U Sports Final 8 basketball championships at the arena at TD Place in Ottawa on fRiday , March 6 , 2020. " data-portal-copyright= " Valerie Wutti " **28;12363;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 568074 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Carleton 82 , Calgary 66&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; They didn&amp;rsquo ; t get to a total of 14 national championships without taking the first step on each occasion . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Carleton Ravens took that step again on Friday , using the force generated by relentless pressure to help them bounce the Calgary Dinos 82-66 in a men&amp;rsquo ; s quarterfinal of the U Sports Final 8 university basketball championships . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Next up for the Ravens are the Western Mustangs , who defeated the Alberta Golden Bears earlier in the day , in a semifinal on Saturday at 6 p.m. at TD Place arena . The winner of that contest will play for the W.P. McGee national championship trophy on Sunday night . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Dinos will be consigned to a consolation-side semifinal against the Golden Bears at the Ravens&amp;rsquo ; Nest on the Carleton campus on Saturday afternoon . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Carleton and Western have met twice previously this season , with the Ravens winning by 25 in a regular-season contest at London , Ont. , and by 22 in the Ontario University Athletics conference final at home on Feb. 29. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We anticipate a very tough matchup . Playing a team a third time is so often difficult , &amp;rdquo ; Ravens head coach Taffe Charles said . &amp;ldquo ; The good news is we don&amp;rsquo ; t think we have to watch very much video right now , so that&amp;rsquo ; s a great . If it was Alberta , we&amp;rsquo ; d have to watch a pile of video . I think it&amp;rsquo ; s just about making adjustments , for them as well . It&amp;rsquo ; s going to be somebody we played last week . We just have to be prepared for them , and we&amp;rsquo ; ll be ready to make some adjustments . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Calgary&amp;rsquo ; s roster featured 2019-20 national &lt;span style= " font-family : -apple-system , BlinkMacSystemFont , ' Segoe UI ' , Roboto , Oxygen-Sans , Ubuntu , Cantarell , ' Helvetica Neue ' , sans-serif ; " &gt; player of the year Brett Layton , who forced Ravens defenders into a series of fouls and did about as much as was humanly possible for his team , posting game-high totals of 23 and 16 rebounds. &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The problem was that Layton didn&amp;rsquo ; t have anywhere close to enough help . Ezeoha Santiago scored 14 points , but no other Dinos player contributed more than six . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Ravens had seven players with more than six points , topped by Isiah Osborne with 20 and Biniam Grebrekidan and all-Canadian rookie of the year Lloyd Pandi both with 12 . Grebrekidan , who shared defensive duty against Layton , also collected 11 rebounds in 27 minutes . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Obviously , there&amp;rsquo ; s a lot of stuff that we still have to work on , minor things that we have to fix , &amp;rdquo ; Osborne said . &amp;ldquo ; I usually just trying to come on the court and do what coach asks me , what the ( other ) players ask me to do . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Friday&amp;rsquo ; s contest was a rematch of sorts . Last March in Halifax , the Ravens blasted the Dinos 83-49 to capture their most recent national title , and they started off the current campaign with an 80-63 preseason victory at a tournament in Victoria . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; On the same court where they suffered their only defeat against a Canadian opponent all season , by one point against the Ottawa Gee-Gees in the Capital Hoops Classic on Feb. 7 , the Ravens took a 19-14 lead over the Dinos in the first quarter and they pushed the advantage to 43-25 after the second . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Calgary twice pulled within 11 points in the third quarter , but Carleton was back in front by 16 as the fourth began and was not in any kind of mood to let that lead slip before the final buzzer. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Layton said the game got away from the Dinos in the second quarter because the squad that won the 2018 championship &amp;mdash ; the only one not claimed by the Ravens since 2011 &amp;mdash ; became undisciplined . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Other than that , we were with them , &amp;rdquo ; Layton said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; So no surprises ? &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; No . Honestly , they&amp;rsquo ; re so disciplined with what they do , &amp;rdquo ; he added . &amp;ldquo ; The way that they play is very disciplined , so we knew what we were going to get into , but what&amp;rsquo ; s hard to scout is how hard they play , and they play harder than anyone in the country . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I&amp;rsquo ; m glad we got to play them this year , get a little more experience against them , and hopefully next year we can get them . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Charles said Ravens players appeared to be a little nervous at the start of Friday&amp;rsquo ; s contest , at least to him . &amp;ldquo ; Hopefully getting this win under our belts will help us relax a little bit and play a little bit better ( Saturday ) . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Most of the statistical differences between the teams on Friday were less than severe , but there was one that stood out : While Carleton was 10-for-20 from three-point range , Calgary was just 4-for-19 ( 21 per cent ) . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; That translated into an 18-point edge for the Ravens , and they won by 16 , so &amp;hellip ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We didn&amp;rsquo ; t expect it to be easy , &amp;rdquo ; Charles said . &amp;ldquo ; Sometimes we make it look easy as a team . We&amp;rsquo ; ve had success in the past . But it&amp;rsquo ; s not easy winning . Winning is not that easy and sometimes we may think it looks easy , but it&amp;rsquo ; s very difficult . " data-portal-copyright= " Tony Caldwell " **28;14902;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 567242 " /&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 100% " height= " 100% " frameborder= " 0 " allowfullscreen= " true " src= " https : //www.youtu ... &gt; &lt;/iframe&gt; &lt;p&gt; Brett Layton of the Calgary Dinos and Jenna Mae Ellsworth of the Prince Edward Island Panthers have been named Canadian university basketball players of the year . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The announcements were made during ceremonies at the Canadian Museum of History on Wednesday night , the eve of the start of the U Sports men&amp;rsquo ; s and women&amp;rsquo ; s championships at TD Place arena . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There was some national capital region flavour to the annual awards , too . Carleton Ravens guard Lloyd Pandi was named men&amp;rsquo ; s rookie of the year as well as a member of the all-rookie and second-team all-Canadian all-star teams , while Gatineau&amp;rsquo ; s Khal&amp;eacute ; ann Caron-Goudreau , a forward with the Laval Rouge et Or , was named women&amp;rsquo ; s defensive player of the year and a second-team all-Canadian. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; As well , Ottawa Gee-Gees guard Calvin Epistola was a first-team men&amp;rsquo ; s all-star , Ottawa&amp;rsquo ; s Brooklynn McAlear-Fanus was a second-team women&amp;rsquo ; s all-star , and Gatineau&amp;rsquo ; s Anthony Tsegakele , a guard for the Brandon Bobcats , was a men&amp;rsquo ; s rookie all-star . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Layton , a fourth-year player and law student , led all Canadian university players with 299 rebounds , and he topped the Canada West conference in field goal percentage ( 62.8 ) and blocked shots ( 43 ) . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Also in her fourth year , Ellsworth led the Panthers with 20.5 points per game while also averaging 5.9 rebounds , 3.2 assists and 2.1 steals per game . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span style= " font-family : -apple-system , BlinkMacSystemFont , ' Segoe UI ' , Roboto , Oxygen-Sans , Ubuntu , Cantarell , ' Helvetica Neue ' , sans-serif ; " &gt;Pandi scored in double digits scoring in all but one game he suited up for this season . His 16.1 points per game , including five of 20-plus points , were tops among Ravens players , and he led U SPORTS by making 66.1 per cent of his field-goal attempts . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The only other Carleton player to be named men&amp;rsquo ; s national rookie of the year was Philip Scrubb in 2011. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Caron-Goudreau , an MBA student in global business , won the women&amp;rsquo ; s defensive player award for the second consecutive year . She was second in the Quebec conference with 1.5 blocked shots per game , and she averaged 10.8 rebounds per contest . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Other major men&amp;rsquo ; s basketball award winners included : Michael Rouault of Thompson Rivers , Ken Shields Award for student-community service ; Lock Lam of Lakehead , top defensive player ; and Rick Plato of Dalhousie , top coach . Carleton&amp;rsquo ; s Taffe Charles was also nominated for the coach of the year award . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Remaining women&amp;rsquo ; s award winners included : Jael Kabunda of Bishops , rookie of the year ; Julia Curran of Western , Sylvia Sweeney Award for student-athlete community service ; Mike Rao of Brock , coach of the year ; and Addison Martin of Manitoba , &amp;nbsp ; Tracy McLeod Award for her courage in overcoming adversity . &lt;/p&gt;
